options.consequence: Shorter, but hides that the ADR also fixes the production provider and every timestamp.

chosen: 003-time-source-virtual-scheduler
why: hsdd-adr asks for a 2 to 4 word kebab slug of the decision topic; this one mirrors the title without 'on Dart', which every ADR in this tree implies. Naming only, no evidence needed.

question: Should the production provider fork Zone.current at bus construction, as the root proposed, or capture Zone.current as it is?

options.label: Capture Zone.current without forking
options.consequence: Zero added cost when the bus runs in its construction zone (root-zone fast paths); same behavior under fakeAsync, withClock and testWidgets; no zone identity of the bus's own.

options.label: Pass-through fork of Zone.current
options.consequence: Gives bus callbacks a distinguishable zone, at about 1.3 times the per-event delivery cost in the root zone; no behavior the captured zone lacks.

chosen: Capture Zone.current without forking
why: The fork intercepts nothing, so it buys only a zone identity no decision uses, and costs about 4 ns per delivered event (28 ms against 37 ms for 2,000,000 events, Q8). The captured zone is driven by fakeAsync when built inside it (Q6) and by tester.pump inside a testWidgets body (W1), exactly as the fork was in time-source-flutter. Signal that would change it: a need to tell bus callbacks apart by zone, such as zone-local diagnostics.

question: Does the production provider read package:clock's clock at each call, or capture it when the bus is constructed?

options.label: Capture clock at bus construction
options.consequence: Timestamps always follow the same clock as the bus's timers, whatever zone a publish comes from; a withClock or fakeAsync around construction governs the bus for its life.

options.label: Read clock at each call
options.consequence: A publish made under a different withClock stamps a clock other than the one the bus's timers follow.

options.label: Capture at BusConfig construction
options.consequence: A config built in main and a bus built later inside a fake zone would disagree with the bus's zone.

chosen: Capture clock at bus construction
why: package:clock's clock is a zone value read at the call site, so per-call reads split the bus's time between its zone and its callers' zones. Q6 shows a captured clock keeps the withClock it was built under and follows fakeAsync when built inside it; W2 shows the captured clock equals clock.now() inside a testWidgets body and advances exactly with tester.pump. Capturing with the zone keeps the pair consistent.

question: Does bus.observe(topic) subscribe inside the provider zone, or return the subject's stream so subscribers keep their own zone (the proposal's item 6: a test's own subscription gets its replay only after a real turn)?

options.label: listen re-enters the provider zone
options.consequence: A TestBus subscriber gets the replayed first value under triggerActions with no await, and timers its chained operators create during delivery are virtual; its callbacks run in the provider zone, so its own zone values and error zone are not visible there.

options.label: Return the subject stream unchanged
options.consequence: Subscribers keep their own zone, but on a TestBus their first replayed value needs a real turn and their delivery-time timers run on real time.

chosen: listen re-enters the provider zone
why: Q2 shows the re-entering stream delivers the replay microtask under triggerActions and runs the consumer's callbacks in the virtual zone, while the raw subject stream needs a real turn. Spec §3.3 has bus.observe subscribe on the topic's dispatcher on Combine, and on Dart the dispatcher is the provider zone, so this is the Spec's own shape. It also makes TestBus synchronous whichever first-delivery timing OQ-R1 picks. Signal that would change it: a consumer that needs its own zone values inside callbacks, such as a zone-scoped logging context.

question: In which zone does the bus invoke observers (Spec §3.7) and create its own timers and microtasks (reentrancy deferral, dev-mode window, grace timer)?

options.label: Explicitly in the provider zone
options.consequence: Deferrals, timers and observer side work are virtual on a TestBus whatever zone the publish or release call arrives from; one zone.run per call, a fast path when already in the zone.

options.label: Zone.current at the call site
options.consequence: A publish or scope release made from a test's own zone would put the deferral or the grace timer outside virtual time.

chosen: Explicitly in the provider zone
why: Q3 shows zone.scheduleMicrotask and zone.run(() => Timer(...)) reach the virtual queue from a call made in another zone, while the global scheduleMicrotask lands in the caller's zone, and the reentrant deferral then restores per-topic order under triggerActions. Spec §3.7 runs observers on the per-topic delivery dispatcher, which on Dart is the provider zone. Observers in the provider zone has no experiment of its own; it follows from the same zone mechanics.

question: RxDart 0.28's switchMap, switching while the previous inner is live, chains on the previous inner's cancel() future, which is the SDK's root-zone null future, so its resubscription escapes the virtual scheduler, fakeAsync and testWidgets. How does the tree keep topology pipelines inside virtual time?

options.label: Live switchMap that does not wait, synchronous operations
options.consequence: nidana.runtime owns one combinator's live implementation (cancel the previous inner, listen the next at once, as RxJS and RxJava do); every topology pipeline then completes inside the provider zone under the virtual scheduler, fakeAsync and testWidgets alike, and Spec §3.6's operations stay synchronous. Deviates from Spec §2.3's 'the bus does not implement stream combinators'.

options.label: Asynchronous scheduler operations
options.consequence: advanceTimeBy, advanceTimeTo and triggerActions return futures and yield a real event-loop turn at every virtual instant: tolerant of any root-zone hop, but every test awaits every operation, each instant costs a real timer, and fakeAsync and testWidgets stay broken.

options.label: RxDart switchMap plus an async settle after every publish
options.consequence: No owned combinator, but the resubscription still misses every virtual instant advanceTimeBy reaches before the next real turn, and never runs inside a testWidgets body.

options.label: Wrap inner subscriptions so cancel returns a provider-zone future
options.consequence: Keeps RxDart's switchMap, but needs to recognize the SDK's private null future by identity and wraps every inner stream; fragile against SDK changes.

chosen: Live switchMap that does not wait, synchronous operations
why: Q1 shows RxDart's switchMap listens to the next inner only after a real turn, at whatever virtual time has been reached by then; Q9 and W4 show the next inner is never listened within a fakeAsync block or a testWidgets body, even 300 ms of fake time later. A no-wait switchMap keeps exact virtual timing in all three (Q1, Q9, W4b). The SDK defines the null future with Zone.root.run in dart:_internal, so no zone can capture the hop. Only switchMap among the Spec §6.3 combinators chains on a cancel future in RxDart 0.28. Root D6 already wraps every combinator in the DSL, so owning one live implementation adds little; Spec §6.3 asks switchMap only to cancel the previous async work. Close call against asynchronous operations; the signal that would have changed my mind: a second live combinator whose work cannot be kept inside the provider zone. Marked for upstreaming because of Spec §2.3.

question: Do the topology DSL's time-dependent combinators stay RxDart's operators (proposal item 4), now that periodic operators and cancellation are tested?

options.label: RxDart operators inside the pipeline, no scheduler argument
options.consequence: No reimplementation; every timer they create, periodic included, is a provider-zone timer, and cancelling the pipeline cancels it.

options.label: Reimplement against an abstract scheduler
options.consequence: Contradicts Spec §2.3 and duplicates RxDart, for no behavior the zone does not already give.

chosen: RxDart operators inside the pipeline, no scheduler argument
why: Q1 drives debounceTime, throttleTime, delay, sampleTime and bufferTime (both on Stream.periodic), Stream.timeout, interval and Rx.retryWhen with a timed retry by virtual time alone, with no real-time emission, and cancelling each leaves no timer. W6 shows a debounce subscription cancelled in dispose leaves nothing pending under testWidgets. The proposal's choice stands with broader evidence.

question: Is VirtualScheduler nidana's own implementation, or a wrapper over package:fake_async, and does any nidana package depend on fake_async?

options.label: Own implementation, no fake_async dependency
options.consequence: About 200 lines in testing.dart (the prototype is in the experiment); Spec §3.6 names, a fixed start instant, a runaway bound and pending-timer inspection under nidana's control; ADR-002's dependency table holds.

options.label: Wrap fake_async
options.consequence: Mature and already in every Flutter resolution, but adds a dependency to a published package, starts at the wall clock by default, never returns from elapse on a zero-period periodic timer, and has the same root-zone hop.

chosen: Own implementation, no fake_async dependency
why: ADR-002 item 3 lists the runtime's dependencies without fake_async; the prototype implements every operation and passes the drain, periodic, bound and error cases (Q4); fake_async's elapse spun 817 million times on a zero-period periodic timer without returning (output-fake-async.txt). Signal that would change it: nidana's scheduler failing a timer case fake_async already handles.

question: What do triggerActions, advanceTimeBy and advanceTimeTo do with microtasks (replay, Spec §3.4 deferral) and periodic timers, and how does a test observe quiescence?

options.label: Event-loop order, monotonic time, bounded, quiescent on return
options.consequence: Microtasks FIFO before each timer, timers by due time then creation; periodic timers fire once per period crossed; negative or backward moves throw ArgumentError; reentrant calls and runaway drains throw StateError; every operation returns quiescent, with pending timers inspectable; errors go to the scheduler's construction error zone.

options.label: fake_async semantics
options.consequence: Similar ordering, but wall-clock start, no runaway bound, no notion of returning quiescent beyond flushTimers.

options.label: RxJava TestScheduler semantics
options.consequence: advanceTimeTo may move time backward; microtasks have no counterpart.

chosen: Event-loop order, monotonic time, bounded, quiescent on return
why: Q4 shows the prototype reproduces the real event loop's order (m1, m3, t1, m2, t3, t2), fires equal-due timers in creation order and a timer created mid-advance within the advance, fires a 300 ms periodic timer three times over one second, rejects backward and negative moves, and turns a microtask loop and a zero-period timer into StateError. Errors reach the error zone the scheduler was built in, not the caller's (Q4), which the ADR states because tests construct the TestBus in the test body. The fixed default start instant and the bound's value are left to bus-testing@v1.

question: Is the virtual clock also package:clock's clock inside the virtual zone?

options.label: Yes, fork the zone under withClock(virtualClock)
options.consequence: Shell code a bus callback runs that reads clock.now() sees virtual time, consistent with the bus's stamps; costs nothing.

options.label: No, only the provider clock is virtual
options.consequence: Code in bus callbacks that reads package:clock sees the wall clock while the bus stamps virtual time.

chosen: Yes, fork the zone under withClock(virtualClock)
why: Q5 shows clock.now() inside the zone reads virtual time and outside it the system clock; fake_async does the same in its run, so apps already expect it. No option has a cost beyond one zone value.

question: How does a TestBus test handle work that starts outside the provider zone (a stub future the test completes, RxDart operators an app chains), and what is the settle() of an ADR-001 harness over a TestBus?

options.label: bus-testing@v1 adds an asynchronous settle
options.consequence: Alternates triggerActions with real event-loop turns until quiescent across a turn, bounded; ADR-001 harnesses use it; it needs a real event loop, so never inside fakeAsync or testWidgets.

options.label: Tests yield by hand
options.consequence: No new operation, but every test author must know to await once before triggerActions, and harnesses reimplement it.

chosen: bus-testing@v1 adds an asynchronous settle
why: Q7 shows a stub completed from the test zone is not delivered by triggerActions alone, and is delivered by one awaited turn followed by triggerActions or by the prototype settle. ADR-001 already requires a Future<void> settle() on every harness, so the operation has a consumer from day one.

question: Which provider may a TestBus have, and can widget tests record envelopes?

options.label: TestBus is always virtual; the recorder attaches to any bus
options.consequence: TestBus(config) takes config's VirtualSchedulerProvider or a fresh one and rejects a production provider with ArgumentError; widget tests attach the recorder to a production-provider bus, as the root's runtime-to-flutter edge requires.

options.label: TestBus accepts any provider
options.consequence: A TestBus could then be non-deterministic, against Spec Appendix A.7's definition.

options.label: Recorder only on TestBus
options.consequence: Widget tests, which run the production provider, could not record envelopes.

chosen: TestBus is always virtual; the recorder attaches to any bus
why: Spec Appendix A.7 defines TestBus by its VirtualSchedulerProvider; the root DAG says widget tests record envelopes on a real bus (runtime to flutter, bus-testing@v1 hard), and W1 shows widget tests need the production provider for tester.pump to drive time. The recorder is an observer, so attaching it to any bus costs nothing.

question: How do Flutter widget tests construct and shut down the bus, given that flutter_test fails a test whose fake timers are still pending after it unmounts the tree?

options.label: Build in the body, shut down from an ancestor's dispose
options.consequence: The helpers construct the bus inside the test body and shut it down from the dispose of a widget above every scope binding, after the bindings released their references; a test with its own bus shuts it down before the body ends.

options.label: Shut down in tearDown, as Spec §11.2 says
options.consequence: Fails every widget test that leaves a grace or dev-mode timer pending, because the pending-timer check runs before tear-downs.

options.label: Build in setUp
options.consequence: setUp runs outside the body's fake zone, so tester.pump never drives the bus.

chosen: Build in the body, shut down from an ancestor's dispose
why: pending_timer_test.dart fails with 'A Timer is still pending even after the widget tree was disposed' although an addTearDown would cancel the timer; W5 shows the unmount disposes descendants first, so a grace timer a module binding starts in its dispose is cancelled by an ancestor's shutdown and nothing stays pending; W3 shows a bus built in setUp is not driven by tester.pump. The helpers cannot take a WidgetTester (ADR-002 item 4) and need none for this. Marked for upstreaming: Spec §11.2's test row says tearDown.

question: What does a zero grace period do, and what does shutdown do with timers?

options.label: Zero grace tears down synchronously; shutdown cancels every timer
options.consequence: No zero-duration timer to drain; after shutdown no bus or pipeline timer is pending, which flutter_test requires and TestBus inspection can assert.

options.label: Zero grace as a zero-duration timer
options.consequence: Teardown waits for the next drain or event-loop turn, which Spec §7.3's 'immediately' does not describe.

chosen: Zero grace tears down synchronously; shutdown cancels every timer
why: Spec §7.3 says a grace period of 0 tears down immediately on the last release. Shutdown cancelling timers follows from the flutter_test invariant (pending_timer_test.dart, W5); pipeline timers go with their subscriptions (Q1 cancellation counts, W6).

question: Is the set of scheduler providers closed (production and virtual), or may applications implement SchedulerProvider?

options.label: Closed set of two
options.consequence: The bus can rely on quiescence and cancellation rules; an application that wants its own timers and clock constructs the bus inside its own zone.

options.label: Open interface
options.consequence: Applications can plug in other fake-time systems, and can break the rules the bus and TestBus rely on.

chosen: Closed set of two
why: Spec §3.6 names only the real-time default and the virtual provider. Because the production provider captures the construction zone and clock, a custom zone already reaches the bus without a custom provider (Q6). Judgement beyond that; signal that would change it: an adopter integrating a time system that cannot be expressed as a zone.

question: How does shell code outside the runtime (navigation executors stamping RouteTransition, the telemetry observer) get the bus's time without DateTime.now()?

options.label: bus-api@v1 exposes the provider clock read-only
options.consequence: Executors and services stamp from the same clock as envelopes, virtual on a TestBus and fake under testWidgets; the contract fixes the accessor's shape.

options.label: Shell code reads package:clock itself
options.consequence: Correct only when the call happens to run inside the provider zone or the right withClock.

chosen: bus-api@v1 exposes the provider clock read-only
why: Guide §3.4 has the executor write RouteTransition with a timestamp, Spec Appendix A.6 makes it part of the confirmed transition, and Q6 shows a call-site clock read can diverge from the captured one. No experiment compares accessor shapes; that is the bus-api@v1 author's choice.

question: Does ADR-003 settle the Dart topic model's dispatcher hint (nidana.model's OQ-M3), or only the dispatcher's meaning?

options.label: State the dispatcher, leave OQ-M3 to the model
options.consequence: The ADR fixes one dispatcher per bus, the provider zone, and no hop in bus.observe; whether topic-model@v1 omits the hint or accepts and ignores it stays with its contract step.

options.label: Resolve OQ-M3 here by omitting the field
options.consequence: Settles a topic-model@v1 surface question in an ADR that does not govern topic-model@v1, and pre-empts the model's compile-compatibility option.

chosen: State the dispatcher, leave OQ-M3 to the model
why: Spec §3.6's table already gives Dart's dispatcher as the isolate event loop, and OQ-M3 asks a surface question (omit, or accept and ignore) whose cost lands on topic-model@v1's consumers. Keeping topic-model@v1 out of affects keeps ADR-003 out of tooling phase contexts. Judgement; no experiment applies.

question: Which nodes and contracts does ADR-003 affect (the proposal listed nidana.runtime, nidana.navigation, nidana.flutter, nidana.integration, bus-api@v1, bus-testing@v1)?

options.label: Proposal's set plus nidana.model, navigation-api@v1, flutter-binding@v1
options.consequence: Model phases get the rule that the contracts package reads no clock and takes timestamps and ids as arguments; the executor protocol and the widget-test helpers carry their ADR-003 obligations; navigation-api@v1 and flutter-binding@v1 consumers are already governed, so no extra phase context grows except the model's.

options.label: Proposal's set
options.consequence: The model's lineage functions and the two downstream contracts would follow ADR-003 without being governed by it.

options.label: Also topic-model@v1 and topology-dsl@v1
options.consequence: Injects ADR-003 into every phase that consumes them, nidana.tooling's included, where it says nothing relevant.

chosen: Proposal's set plus nidana.model, navigation-api@v1, flutter-binding@v1
why: Spec §3.5's own pseudo-code stamps timestamp = now() inside a combinator, the likeliest place for a DateTime.now() default in the model's lineage functions, so the model is bound by item 8. Item 7 binds flutter-binding@v1's widget-test helpers, item 8 binds navigation-api@v1's executor protocol. The live switchMap rule sits in bus-api@v1, which declares the live builder (ADR-001 item 4), so topology-dsl@v1 stays out. Signal that would change it: topic-model@v1 making timestamp a required argument with no default, which would let nidana.model drop out.

question: Which spec lines does accepting ADR-003 change, beyond the proposal pointer and Governed by?

options.label: Update the lines the ADR changes
options.consequence: nidana.runtime's Owns names the live switchMap and its Inherited line states the zone rules; nidana.flutter's widget-test library bullet states construction in the body and shutdown at unmount; root OQ7's detail summarizes the accepted decision; nidana.model gains Governed by ADR-003 in its file and in the root's block.

options.label: Pointer and Governed by only
options.consequence: nidana.runtime's Owns list, which its own decomposition divides, would not show that the runtime owns a live switchMap.

chosen: Update the lines the ADR changes
why: The runtime's hsdd-spec step divides its Owns list, so an ownership the ADR creates must appear there; the flutter line now carries an obligation the phase plan must schedule. OQ2's detail already pointed at ADR-003 for clock control and stays PARTIAL on OQ-R2; OQ7's row was already RESOLVED pointing at ADR-003.

question: Which of nidana.model's declarations belong to topic-model@v1, and which to topology-dsl@v1 and topology-ir@v1?

options.label: shared values here, API and IR elsewhere
options.consequence: topic-model@v1 holds topics, TopicRef, the name predicate, MessageEnvelope, MessageSource, Lineage, Scope, the observer seam and RedactedPayload; topology-dsl@v1 holds Topology, the builder, the stream handle, combinators, the recorder and buildDefinition(); topology-ir@v1 holds the IR, its JSON form (including the encodings of TopicRef, Scope and MessageSource), graphs, renderers and every analysis over sets of definitions

options.label: IR-adjacent values in topology-ir, observers in bus-api
options.consequence: TopicRef and Scope would version with the IR and the observer seam with the runtime, so every app declaring topics or observers would couple to contracts it otherwise does not use, and the DSL contract would depend on the IR contract for Scope

chosen: shared values here, API and IR elsewhere
why: The root contract matrix names app code declaring topics and observers as topic-model@v1's external consumers, and Scope and TopicRef cross the DSL, the IR and bus-api@v1. The placement rule written into the contract: a value crossing more than one of the three contracts, or one an app constructs without declaring a topology, lives here; an analysis over a collection of definitions lives in topology-ir@v1 even when it compares values defined here.

question: Does topic-model@v1 get a public library of its own, or does it live in the package's main library?

options.label: main library only
options.consequence: one import for apps and fixtures; the topic-model fixtures compile only once the main library exists, which fp-progression lands in nidana.model's first phase anyway

options.label: per-contract libraries exported by the main library
options.consequence: a consumer could import topic-model alone; three more public libraries to keep in step with three contracts

chosen: main library only
why: ADR-002 item 3's default; every in-tree consumer of topic-model@v1 also consumes topology-dsl@v1. The text leaves the next two contracts free to name a library of their own. Signal that would change it: a consumer needing the topic model without the DSL's names, for instance a name collision with an app type.

question: Do produced_by and consumers name node ids or guessed first phase ids while no phase plan exists?

options.label: node ids
options.consequence: every id resolves in the tree today; hsdd-reconcile replaces them through confirm entries

options.label: guessed first phase ids
options.consequence: nidana.model.1 is near certain, but nidana.runtime and nidana.tooling are internal nodes whose consuming phases belong to children not yet minted, so their ids cannot be guessed, and the producer delivers this contract over several phases

chosen: node ids
why: Two of the five consumers are internal nodes, and a shared-model contract is produced over more than one phase (skeleton, then the pure functions), so a phase-id guess would be wrong more often than not. phase_ids: provisional carries the state.

question: Does the contract header list ADR-003 under Governed by?

options.label: ADR-001 and ADR-002 only
options.consequence: matches the affects lists; ADR-003 item 8 is cited in prose and enforced by G12 and G25

options.label: add ADR-003
options.consequence: a Governed-by link the ADR's own affects list does not reciprocate

chosen: ADR-001 and ADR-002 only
why: ADR-003's affects lists nidana.model, not topic-model@v1, and the ADR's links are hsdd-adr's to change. If the owner wants the reciprocal link, an hsdd-adr touch adds topic-model@v1 to ADR-003's affects and then this header gains ADR-003.

question: OQ-M3: does the Dart topic model carry Spec §3.6's per-topic dispatcher hint at all?

options.label: omit the field
options.consequence: a declaration with a dispatcher argument does not compile (G5); nothing suggests a hint that cannot work

options.label: accept it and ignore it
options.consequence: declarations translated from Kotlin compile, but a field with no effect reads as moving work off the UI isolate

chosen: omit the field
why: ADR-003 item 9 makes the provider zone the one dispatcher of every topic of a bus; Spec §3.6 and §11.1 make the hint advisory ('where supported'); ports are out of v1 (root D1) and consume the Specification, not this tree (root D2). Signal that would change it: a v1 requirement to compile topic declarations shared with another platform.

question: Is MessageEnvelope.source a String, as Spec §2.4 shows it, or a typed value?

options.label: sealed MessageSource
options.consequence: five final variants (topology, service, page, executor, unknown) that render the Spec's format with toString() and parse back with tryParse; a malformed source does not compile; bus-api@v1's publisher factory takes a MessageSource

options.label: String
options.consequence: literal Spec shape; any string is accepted and the format is checked nowhere

chosen: sealed MessageSource
why: Spec §1 'typed over stringly-typed' and the owner's ADT preference; Spec §2.4 fixes a closed format. Signal that would change it: a needed source kind outside the four the Spec names, which would make the closed family a breaking change each time.

question: Is envelope lineage computed per pipeline stage, as Spec §3.5 describes (a fresh envelope and id at every stage), or per published message?

options.label: per published message
options.consequence: single-input, time-shifting and accumulator stages pass their input's Lineage through; only combine and withLatestFrom make a new one; ids and timestamps are minted at publish; every published causationId names a published envelope; fewer allocations per stage

options.label: per stage, literal Spec §3.5
options.consequence: a chain of two stages publishes an envelope whose causationId names an intermediate envelope no observer, recorder or devtool can see, so the causation chain cannot be walked

chosen: per published message
why: Intermediate envelopes are invisible (Spec §3.5 'Where Envelopes Are Visible'), and Spec §2.4's purpose for causationId is walking the chain backward. The two readings agree on every one-stage pipeline and differ only where the literal one breaks tracing. topology-dsl@v1 must adopt this mapping per combinator.

question: What is the sensitive flag of an envelope published to a topic when its inputs differ: the destination topic's flag (Spec §2.4) or the flag propagated through the pipeline (Spec §3.5)?

options.label: mirror the destination topic
options.consequence: published sensitive == topic.sensitive; the lineage carries the propagated flag for diagnostics only; a non-sensitive topic derived from a sensitive one is visible to non-sensitive observers

options.label: taint
options.consequence: published sensitive is the topic's flag or any input's; every topic downstream of auth state, the navigation resolver's resolved intents included, disappears from non-sensitive observers

chosen: mirror the destination topic
why: Spec §2.4 defines the field as the published-to topic's flag, and Spec §9.2 places the discipline in flagging topics, backed by the v1 sensitive-type lint. Taint would hide most of an app's traffic from logging. The two Spec sections disagree when a combine stage publishes directly. Signal that would change it: an owner or compliance requirement (PCI scope) that derived data be hidden by default.

question: How does a value read from a Tracing.disabled topic enter lineage?

options.label: lineage-neutral root without a correlation
options.consequence: Lineage.root() contributes no correlation and no parents to a combine; a pipeline fed only by untraced topics starts a new flow at publish

options.label: root with a minted correlation
options.consequence: every combine of a traced and an untraced input becomes cross-correlation, so flows lose their grouping and gain parents no published envelope carries

options.label: a separate untraced envelope type
options.consequence: a sealed envelope family that observers, which never see untraced topics, would still have to match on

chosen: lineage-neutral root without a correlation
why: Guide §8.1 says observability tooling does not see an untraced topic; how the runtime carries untraced values stays bus-api@v1's. The neutral root keeps flow grouping intact.
evidence: docs/auto-run/experiments/topic-model-fixtures/ (G19 case 'inputs without a correlation id contribute none')

question: How do the pure lineage functions obtain a fresh correlation id, given that nidana_dart_contracts generates no id (ADR-003 item 8)?

options.label: a String Function() argument
options.consequence: called only in the cross-correlation case and when a lineage has no correlation at publish, exactly once (G14, G19); the generator stays the caller's

options.label: a String value always supplied
options.consequence: total and simple, but the runtime mints an id for every combine emission and every publish whether used or not

options.label: an outcome value telling the caller to mint
options.consequence: purest, but every caller handles a two-variant result and threads the minted id back in

chosen: a String Function() argument
why: Mints only when the rule needs a fresh id, and the exactly-once behavior is pinned by behavior cases. Signal that would change it: nidana.model's gates forbidding any callback in the pure package.

question: When inputs of a combine share one correlation id, which parent correlation ids does the output carry?

options.label: union in input order
options.consequence: no input's lineage is lost; equals the Spec's worked example when the inputs carry none

options.label: the trigger's only
options.consequence: matches the single-input rule but drops the other inputs' parents

chosen: union in input order
why: Spec §2.4's example only shows empty parents; the union never loses lineage and reduces to the example. No evidence beyond that.

question: What makes two topics equal?

options.label: variant, name and value type
options.consequence: Spec §2.1's identity plus the variant, so a state topic and an event topic with one name and type are distinct and the runtime reports them as a name collision; initial value, dedup, sensitive, tracing and buffer size take no part

options.label: name and value type
options.consequence: the Spec's pair literally; a state and an event declaration of one name and type would be the same key

options.label: object identity
options.consequence: a non-const duplicate declaration becomes a second key for the same channel

chosen: variant, name and value type
why: Spec §2.1 defines identity as (name, type) and §3.1 keys subjects by the topic; adding the variant keeps keys well defined across variants. Signal that would change it: none expected; the runtime's collision check works by name either way.

question: How does a StateTopic declare a constant or a computed initial value in Dart?

options.label: two const constructors and createInitial()
options.consequence: StateTopic(initial: T) and StateTopic.computed(initial: T Function()); both const, so registries can be const or final; a wrong form does not compile (G3)

options.label: a public sealed Initial ADT
options.consequence: one more exposed type that consumers would only ever call create on

options.label: always a factory
options.consequence: every declaration writes a closure and loses const

chosen: two const constructors and createInitial()
why: Spec §2.5 allows both a constant and a pure factory; Guide Appendix C.3 emits static final declarations and Spec §4.2 shows registries; both forms stay const-capable (confirmed by the surface fixture under the stand-in).

question: What does the topic name predicate accept, and do constructors validate names?

options.label: two or three kebab segments, no constructor check
options.consequence: isWellFormedTopicName encodes Spec §4.4's two patterns literally; const constructors stay const; enforcement is left to diagnostics or checks

options.label: two or more segments
options.consequence: admits deeper hierarchies the Spec does not name

options.label: no predicate
options.consequence: the model's Owns item for the naming pattern goes unimplemented

chosen: two or three kebab segments, no constructor check
why: Spec §4.4 names domain.entity and domain.entity.action; a const constructor cannot run a pattern match. Signal that would change it: an adopting app with four-level names, which would need a breaking change to G11.

question: Is a replay topic's buffer size required and bounded below?

options.label: required bufferSize, asserted at least 1
options.consequence: no unbounded replay by default; a const declaration below 1 does not compile, a non-const one fails an assertion

options.label: optional, unbounded by default
options.consequence: a long-lived replay topic grows without bound

chosen: required bufferSize, asserted at least 1
why: Spec §2.1 defines ReplayTopic as buffering N values and Guide §8.1 names replay buffers as the dominant memory cost. The experiment confirmed the analyzer reports const_eval_throws_exception for a const declaration below 1.

question: Does Dedup offer a custom equality in v1?

options.label: enum of equality and none
options.consequence: Dart's == decides, as Spec §3.12's table says for Dart

options.label: a class with a custom equality function
options.consequence: covers types with unusable ==, at the cost of a generic dedup type on every state topic

chosen: enum of equality and none
why: Spec §3.12 fixes == for Dart; the custom equality is TypeScript's requirement. Signal that would change it: a payload type whose == cannot be fixed.

question: Which constructor arguments of MessageEnvelope are required?

options.label: all but causationId and parents
options.consequence: id, payload, correlationId, timestamp, source and sensitive are required (G12); causationId defaults to null and parents to empty, as Spec §2.4 states

options.label: sensitive defaulted to false
options.consequence: a forgotten flag silently exposes a sensitive envelope to every observer

chosen: all but causationId and parents
why: ADR-003 item 8 requires id and timestamp as arguments; a defaulted sensitive flag would fail open on privacy.

question: How is a sensitive payload redacted, and does an envelope's toString redact it?

options.label: runtime type and 32-bit hashCode, redacted toString
options.consequence: RedactedPayload.of renders '<redacted Type #8hex>'; equal payloads redact alike within a run; MessageEnvelope.toString and redacted() never render a sensitive payload

options.label: cryptographic hash of toString()
options.consequence: stable across runs, but needs a dependency ADR-002 forbids and hashes a rendering that may itself leak

options.label: type only
options.consequence: no way to tell two redacted values apart, against Spec §9.2's 'truncated hash'

chosen: runtime type and 32-bit hashCode, redacted toString
why: Spec §9.2 item 2 prescribes type plus truncated hash and default redaction in dev-mode logs; nidana_dart_contracts depends on meta alone. Caveat stated in the contract: a low-entropy payload stays guessable from a hash of its value.

question: What does the observer seam's span API offer, given that root D1 puts an SDK-neutral telemetry observer implementing Guide §8.2's mapping in v1?

options.label: links by message id at span creation
options.consequence: ObserveContext.span(name, attributes:, links:) with envelope ids; SpanHandle has setAttribute and end; the sink resolves ids to its spans; Guide §8.2's causation-link row is implementable

options.label: no links
options.consequence: the telemetry observer could only put causationId in an attribute, and adding links later would break every sink that implements ObserveContext

chosen: links by message id at span creation
why: First drafted without links; changed when checking D1's telemetry observer against Guide §8.2, whose 'Causation chain' row needs links. Links at creation match how telemetry SDKs take them and name no SDK type.

question: What does an observer holding only observeSensitive receive?

options.label: sensitive envelopes only
options.consequence: each capability admits exactly its class of envelope (G23), as Spec §3.7 comments them

options.label: everything
options.consequence: observeSensitive would imply observeAll

chosen: sensitive envelopes only
why: Spec §3.7 describes observeAll as 'sees non-sensitive topics' and observeSensitive as 'sees sensitive topics'; every Spec example grants both together.

question: Does Guide §4.1's AppError become a library type in topic-model@v1?

options.label: leave it to applications
options.consequence: the contract carries no error type; apps declare their own error topic as Guide §4.1 shows

options.label: ship AppError and ErrorKind
options.consequence: a shared error type every package could publish, outside root D1's scope and the model's Owns

chosen: leave it to applications
why: Neither root D1 nor nidana.model's Owns list it; Guide §4.1 presents it as a pattern. Signal that would change it: nidana.integration needing one error type across packages.

question: kind and compatibility of topic-model@v1

options.label: shared-model, versioned
options.consequence: the root matrix's kind; any change consumers could break on bumps the version

options.label: api, additive-only
options.consequence: most additions here are breaking anyway (new variants break exhaustive switches, new interface members break implementers), so additive-only would be claimed and rarely honored

chosen: shared-model, versioned
why: Root contract matrix recommends shared-model; ADR-001 item 4 treats shared-model and api alike for fixtures; the Versioning section lists which changes break.

question: What does the behavior harness of a shared-model contract supply, and what is the binding named?

options.label: settle only, binding named after the package
options.consequence: cases call the library's declarations directly; one binding, nidana_dart_contracts_test.dart, which imports the package so the replay tool reports PENDING until it exists

options.label: a harness exposing the pure functions
options.consequence: a consumer could bind a stand-in for the lineage and redaction functions, at the cost of cases that reach half the surface through the harness and half directly

chosen: settle only, binding named after the package
why: A value type has no second implementation, and root D10 has consumers build against the real package after the producer's first phase. Signal that would change it: nidana.model's phase plan landing the function signatures without bodies in phase 1 while runtime phases must start.

question: Write hsdd/contract/fixture/analysis_options.yaml as the first contract step?

options.label: write it exactly as ADR-001 item 2 states
options.consequence: no lint set; strict-casts, strict-inference and strict-raw-types on; governs every fixture of every contract

options.label: leave it to a later step
options.consequence: the topic-model fixtures would analyze under the root lint set once a workspace exists, and depend_on_referenced_packages would fire on every import

chosen: write it exactly as ADR-001 item 2 states
why: The step instruction and ADR-001 item 8 assign it to the first hsdd-contract authoring step.

question: Does topic-model@v1 carry a JSON Schema?

options.label: no schema
options.consequence: the Interface's Dart declarations are the schema (ADR-001 item 4); the JSON encodings of TopicRef, Scope and MessageSource go to topology-ir@v1's schema

options.label: a schema for TopicRef and MessageSource
options.consequence: a second home for an encoding the IR's schema must also state

chosen: no schema
why: ADR-001 item 4: api and shared-model contracts carry no schema unless they have a serialized form; this contract has none of its own.

question: S06 suggests an optional hsdd-adr touch that adds topic-model@v1 to ADR-003's affects, so the contract header could carry Governed by ADR-003. Run it?

options.label: Run the hsdd-adr touch
options.consequence: One more step; hsdd-config would inject ADR-003's Decision into every phase that consumes topic-model@v1, which is nearly every phase of the tree.

options.label: Leave affects as it is
options.consequence: ADR-003 keeps governing nidana.model, the producer, so the producer's phases still receive it; the contract carries the obligation as its own guarantee G25 and cites ADR-003 item 8 in prose.

chosen: Leave affects as it is
why: The obligation ADR-003 puts on this contract (no clock, no scheduling, timestamps and ids as arguments) binds the producer, which ADR-003 already governs, and the contract states it as G25. Injecting ADR-003 into every consumer's phase context would add a long Decision to phases it does not constrain. The signal that would change this: a consumer-side obligation from ADR-003 on topic-model values.

question: Which signature makes writing a handle of the wrong value type to a topic a compile error (Spec §4.2), given that Dart generics are covariant and inference solves a type argument two arguments constrain to their least upper bound?

options.label: write<T>(Topic<T>, TopicStream<T>)
options.consequence: the Guide B.3 shape, but an unrelated or a wider stream compiles as write<Object>; Spec §4.2's guarantee does not hold

options.label: write<T, S extends T>(Topic<T>, TopicStream<S>)
options.consequence: keeps the b.write(topic, stream) shape; an unrelated or wider stream is one could_not_infer error, a subtype stream into a supertype topic compiles

options.label: stream.writeTo(topic)
options.consequence: rejects unrelated types, but rejects the sound subtype case and admits the unsound wider case

options.label: b.write(topic).from(stream)
options.consequence: sound and permissive, but a new call shape and a dangling write target when .from is forgotten

options.label: invariant handle via a function-type typedef
options.consequence: sound but rejects sound subtype writes, reports two diagnostics per misuse and exposes an obscure typedef

chosen: write<T, S extends T>(Topic<T>, TopicStream<S>)
why: The probe shows it is the only form that keeps the Spec and Guide call shape while rejecting both unsound cases with a single diagnostic and accepting the sound subtype write. Explicit type arguments that widen T still bypass it; the live publish then fails at run time, which no form avoids.

question: How do the recording and the live implementations of the DSL relate: two implementations of a builder interface, or one recording builder whose plan a live implementation interprets?

options.label: two builder implementations
options.consequence: matches the 'live builder' wording of ADR-001 item 4; declare() runs twice per activation (record for checks, then wire live); handles must be an implementable interface, so a handle from one builder passed to the other fails only at run time and apps can implement handles

options.label: one recording builder, plan interpreted live
options.consequence: declare() runs once; the IR and the live wiring come from one plan by construction; handles, builder and stages are closed types; the runtime implements a StageVisitor over a public plan library; bus-api@v1 declares an activation path, no live builder type

chosen: one recording builder, plan interpreted live
why: The Specification says the bus interprets the recorded declaration (Spec §2.2 'inert data', §2.5 'the bus interprets this metadata on activation', §6.5 'the bus interprets the same IR for live activation, ensuring the graph and the running system are structurally identical', A.1, A.4). Dart has no higher-kinded types, so a builder interface with two implementations cannot type its handles per implementation. The owner's functional-first practice (an immutable ADT and its interpreters, pure core and imperative shell) points the same way. ADR-001 item 4's binding rule still holds: the live binding lives with bus-api@v1, which declares the live implementation. The signal that would have favored two builders: a live behavior the plan cannot express, which no Spec §6.3 combinator needs.

question: OQ-M2: How does live activation obtain the transformers a pure-data IR names?

options.label: executable beside FunctionRef in the IR
options.consequence: matches the Spec wording, but the IR holds functions excluded from equality and JSON, so it is no longer pure data

options.label: record, then run declare() again live
options.consequence: the IR stays pure, but every activation runs declare twice and relies on its determinism for the checked IR to equal what is wired

options.label: one plan, IR projected from it
options.consequence: declare runs once into a TopologyPlan holding the functions; activation checks plan.definition and interprets the same plan; the IR stays pure data

chosen: one plan, IR projected from it
why: It keeps both properties the two original options trade against each other: a pure-data IR and a single declare run, so the checked definition and the live wiring cannot disagree. Recorded as Refinement 3 and G18. nidana.model's phase planning marks the OQ-M2 row.

question: OQ-M1, DSL side: does every combinator take an explicit transformer name?

options.label: explicit name parameter
options.consequence: stable names under --obfuscate and for closures, at the cost of a parameter on every combinator

options.label: no name parameter; the plan keeps the function
options.consequence: the plan holds each function identical to what was passed, and topology-ir@v1 derives FunctionRef from it; closures and obfuscated builds need its fallback

chosen: no name parameter; the plan keeps the function
why: Spec §6.2 asks for named standalone functions, whose tear-off toString() carries the name in JIT and AOT without obfuscation, and the build-time catalog runs on the VM. TopologyBuilder and TopicStream are final, so adding an optional name parameter later is compatible. The signal that would favor the parameter: an owner need for transformer names in an obfuscated release build's runtime graph. The derivation rule and its fallback remain for topology-ir@v1.

question: What is the Dart surface of a topology and its combinators: builder functions only, or methods on the handle, and how closed are the types?

options.label: builder functions only
options.consequence: the Kotlin form combine(a, b, f), map(s, f); no chaining

options.label: Spec and Guide split
options.consequence: read, write, reduceInto, combineN, combineAll and merge on the builder; single-input combinators and withLatestFrom on the handle (Spec §6.1 .map, Guide B.3 a.withLatestFrom, a.switchMap); Topology an @immutable abstract base class with a @nonVirtual buildDefinition(); TopologyBuilder final; TopicStream sealed

chosen: Spec and Guide split
why: It follows Spec §6.1 and Guide B.3's Dart rows, wrapped per root D6. Topology is a base class so no type can implement it with a definition unrelated to its declaration (Spec §6.5); the cost is that a subclass is declared final class, where Guide §6.3's Dart example writes class. Arities: combine2 to combine4 with combineAll, withLatestFrom to withLatestFrom3, which covers the Guide §3.4 resolver; nesting or combineAll covers more.

question: Which combinators does the v1 DSL provide beyond the Spec §6.3 table, and how are the Spec's error operators (retryWhen, catchError, onErrorResumeNext) realized on Dart?

options.label: Spec §6.3 table plus the three named error operators
options.consequence: a pipeline-level retryWhen must re-subscribe a shared upstream, which is ill-defined for event topics and for shared stages; onErrorResumeNext duplicates catchError for the Guide §4 use

options.label: curated: table, merge, timeout, catchError, retry on switchMap
options.consequence: merge lets a reducer fold several event topics; timeout is a Spec §3.6 time operator; catchError turns a shell failure into a value; retry belongs to the switchMap inner stream, where the effect is, as a pure policy timed on the provider clock

chosen: curated: table, merge, timeout, catchError, retry on switchMap
why: Errors in a DSL pipeline originate in shell streams (Spec §6.3 'effectful stream sources'), so retrying means calling the stream factory again, which is what the switchMap retry does; ADR-003 item 4 anticipates a timed retry. onErrorResumeNext's documented use, fallback state (Guide §4), is catchError. merge is not in Spec §6.3's table but is needed for reducers over several event sources and has trivial lineage; recorded for upstreaming with the error-operator mapping.

question: Does the DSL provide a switch that selects among topic pipelines (Spec §6.1 and §7.1 'switchMap ... to select between pipelines'), beside switchMap over a shell stream factory?

options.label: switchAmong(candidates, select)
options.consequence: expresses the Spec's wording directly, but a selected candidate either is re-subscribed cold, which breaks stage sharing (G27) and runs shared effects twice, or stays shared and hot, which loses a state candidate's current value on selection or replays a past event

options.label: no selecting switch
options.consequence: selection between state-like pipelines is a combine over the configuration topic; between event pipelines, a withLatestFrom gate per pipeline joined by merge; both pipelines stay subscribed

chosen: no selecting switch
why: The stand-in live implementation showed the conflict between a switch among shared stages and the replay semantics of reads; existing combinators express both selection cases exactly. This reverses the inclusion I had first drafted. The signal that would bring it back: a pipeline whose inactive branch is expensive to keep subscribed. Spec §6.1, §7.1 and Guide §10.4 describe the selection as switchMap; recorded for upstreaming.

question: What does an unhandled error in a live pipeline do on Dart, where a stream error does not end the stream?

options.label: the sink it reaches ends
options.consequence: matches Spec §10.2's model (an error terminates the pipeline, the bus logs it in dev mode and does not restart it) and Rx engines on other platforms; the topology's other sinks go on

options.label: the error is reported and the pipeline goes on
options.consequence: more resilient, but a topology would behave differently on Dart than the Specification describes

chosen: the sink it reaches ends
why: Spec §10.2 items 2 and 4 describe termination, and nidana.runtime already owns 'dev-mode logging of terminated pipelines'. The error is never rethrown; reporting goes to the D8 sink. The signal that would favor going on: an owner preference for Dart-native resilience over parity with the Specification.

question: Is a stage evaluated once for all its consumers, or once per consumer, in a live activation?

options.label: shared within an activation
options.consequence: a function runs once per input value and a switchMap's shell factory once per outer value; fan-out order is defined; the runtime must connect reads after wiring every consumer

options.label: one chain per consumer
options.consequence: the Rx default for cold streams; a stage used twice runs its function twice and its shell effect twice

chosen: shared within an activation
why: A switchMap into a service's stream factory consumed by two sinks would otherwise call the service twice, an effect the topology author cannot see; Spec §3.3's fan-out guarantee presupposes one emission feeding several outputs. Connection after wiring makes activation-time replays reach every consumer, whichever first-delivery timing OQ-R1 picks.

question: Which sinks does Spec §3.3's fan-out order cover?

options.label: every sink one emission reaches
options.consequence: the order would depend on how many stages lie between the emission and each sink, which an implementation cannot keep in declaration order without global scheduling

options.label: sinks that take the same handle
options.consequence: the Spec's 'single transformer produces emissions to multiple output topics'; deliverable by subscribing sinks in declaration order

chosen: sinks that take the same handle
why: Spec §3.3 states the guarantee for one transformer's emissions; a sink behind another stage receives a different transformer's output.

question: What does recording do with a stage that reaches no sink?

options.label: record it
options.consequence: Spec §6.5's 'captures all calls'; the definition then shows a read that nothing live performs

options.label: prune it
options.consequence: the definition matches the live wiring, but a forgotten write passes silently

options.label: reject the declaration
options.consequence: planOf throws StateError; a forgotten write fails at activation and in the catalog; conditional wiring on a build-time flag must keep its read inside the condition

chosen: reject the declaration
why: A handle that feeds nothing is almost always a forgotten write, and rejecting it keeps the definition and the live wiring identical. The signal that would favor pruning: topology modules that routinely build handles under build-time flags.

question: Where does the plan library live?

options.label: in the main library
options.consequence: every topology module sees stages, visitors and planOf

options.label: a second public library, topology_plan.dart
options.consequence: a topology module, importing the main library alone, cannot name a stage or obtain a plan (G2); the runtime, tooling and tests import both

chosen: a second public library, topology_plan.dart
why: Only interpreters, the catalog and tests read plans; ADR-002 item 3 lets a contract name a further public library of its package.

question: Is ADR-003 item 3's live switchMap property (cancel the previous inner without waiting, listen to the next at once) a guarantee of topology-dsl@v1 or of bus-api@v1?

options.label: topology-dsl@v1
options.consequence: the property sits with the combinator it constrains, is observable through the live harness without bus types, and is bound by the live binding bus-api@v1 writes

options.label: bus-api@v1
options.consequence: bus-api@v1 would restate switchMap's semantics in its own suite

chosen: topology-dsl@v1
why: It is a property of a combinator this contract defines; the live binding of this suite runs it anyway (G22). The case checks synchronously after a virtual advance with a cancel future that never completes, so both RxDart 0.28's wait and its root-zone hop fail it (run.sh T11).

question: What do the time-dependent combinators emit, given that ADR-003 item 4 makes them RxDart 0.28's operators or Stream.timeout?

options.label: RxDart and SDK semantics as they are
options.consequence: sample and buffer periods count from the first value; throttle is leading only; timeout raises one error per silence; buffer emits empty lists after its first window

options.label: those semantics, with buffer never emitting an empty batch
options.consequence: the runtime drops RxDart's empty windows; every batch has a value whose lineage it carries

chosen: those semantics, with buffer never emitting an empty batch
why: Read from the sources: RxDart 0.28 BufferStreamTransformer passes ignoreEmptyWindows: false and sample and buffer use WindowStrategy.firstEventOnly; throttleTime defaults to leading: true, trailing: false; the SDK's Stream.timeout arms a one-shot timer re-armed only by an input event and captures Zone.current when timeout() is called. An empty batch has no lineage and is noise for batching analytics (Spec §6.3).

question: What lineage does a value carry that catchError produces from an error, and that a read delivers for a state topic's declared initial value?

options.label: always Lineage.root()
options.consequence: simple, but a recovered failure no longer points at the value that caused it

options.label: the most recent value through the stage
options.consequence: trivial to implement, but a switchMap failure would point at the previous query

options.label: the lineage the raising stage would have passed
options.consequence: a recovered value's cause is the input that failed; errors without such a value (timeout, raw operator) recover as a new flow; the runtime carries lineage with each error internally and unwraps it for recover and for raw operators

chosen: the lineage the raising stage would have passed
why: Causation exists to answer 'why did this happen' (Spec §2.4); for a failure the answer is the value whose processing failed. A state topic's initial value was caused by no message, so a read delivers it with Lineage.root(), which topic-model@v1 leaves unstated.

question: Which stages mediate an intra-topology self-reference (Spec §3.8) for topology-ir@v1's analysis?

options.label: scan and reduceInto only
options.consequence: the Spec's explicit example; time-shifting chains that cannot loop in zero time are rejected

options.label: scan, reduceInto, and debounce, delay, sample and buffer with a positive duration
options.consequence: follows the Spec's second clause, 'a stateful operator chain that cannot loop back to the read in zero time'; the IR must carry those durations

chosen: scan, reduceInto, and debounce, delay, sample and buffer with a positive duration
why: Those stages emit only on a timer, so a write fed back to their read cannot re-enter them within one instant; throttle emits its leading value synchronously and does not qualify. The signal that would narrow it: topology-ir@v1 choosing not to carry durations, in which case it treats them as not mediating.

question: What does the raw-engine escape hatch hand the author: envelopes or pipeline values?

options.label: Stream<MessageEnvelope<T>>
options.consequence: the Spec §3.5 wording, but the author would mint ids and timestamps the contracts package cannot provide, and intermediate envelopes are invisible by topic-model@v1's per-published-message rule

options.label: Stream<PipelineValue<T>> with a fresh-correlation source
options.consequence: the author applies topic-model@v1's Lineage functions; errors arrive as the objects stages raised

chosen: Stream<PipelineValue<T>> with a fresh-correlation source
why: topic-model@v1 computes lineage per published message, and nidana_dart_contracts mints no id and reads no clock (topic-model@v1 G25); a Lineage.combine in a raw operator needs a correlation source, which the live implementation provides. Recorded for upstreaming: Spec §3.5's escape hatch on Dart applies lineage functions rather than constructing envelopes.

question: OQ-R3 (nidana.runtime), DSL side: what does a read deliver under the per-read dedup opt-out, and does this contract fix where dedup sits?

options.label: read semantics only
options.consequence: this contract fixes what each read delivers (G19, Dedup.none delivering an equal publish); where suppression sits and what observers see stay with bus-api@v1

options.label: also fix the placement
options.consequence: this contract would decide observer and recorder visibility, which are bus-api@v1's guarantees

chosen: read semantics only
why: What a read delivers is DSL semantics; what an observer sees is the publish path's. Either placement OQ-R3 lists satisfies G19.

question: How are the conformance cases organized so that both the recording and the live implementation can be bound, without this contract naming bus types?

options.label: one library, one harness
options.consequence: the harness would need both recording and live capabilities, and the recording binding could not supply the live ones

options.label: two libraries, two harnesses
options.consequence: recording_conformance.dart (RecordingHarness, settle only) bound here; live_conformance.dart (LiveTopologyHarness with LiveRun: start, publish, watch, deliveries, current, advance, activate, deactivate, settle) bound by bus-api@v1's step

chosen: two libraries, two harnesses
why: Recording and live guarantees need different capabilities; ADR-001 item 4 allows several conformance libraries per contract, and its binding rule puts the live binding with bus-api@v1. The live harness is stated in topic-model and topology-dsl types and Duration only; a stand-in binding on a virtual scheduler passed all 43 live cases.

question: What is the recording binding named?

options.label: nidana_dart_contracts_test.dart
options.consequence: S06's name, after the package

options.label: topology_builder_test.dart
options.consequence: named after the implementation it binds, as ADR-001 item 4 asks; S06's implementation was the package's declarations themselves

chosen: topology_builder_test.dart
why: The implementation here is the recording builder, TopologyBuilder; ADR-001 item 4 names a binding after its implementation. No evidence beyond that rule.

question: Does topology-dsl@v1's Governed by list ADR-003, whose affects omits this contract while its items 3 and 4 constrain it?

options.label: [ADR-001, ADR-002]
options.consequence: agrees with every ADR's affects; G22 and G23 cite ADR-003 items in their text

options.label: [ADR-001, ADR-002, ADR-003]
options.consequence: names the ADR that constrains the switchMap and time guarantees, but disagrees with ADR-003's affects until an hsdd-adr touch adds the contract

why: As S06 did, Governed by mirrors the ADRs' affects; the fix is an ADR-003 touch through hsdd-adr, after which this line gains ADR-003. The signal that would change it: an orchestrator convention that Governed by lists every ADR the text cites.

question: What do produced_by, consumers and external_consumers name?

options.label: node ids, provisional
options.consequence: S06's rule; phase planning confirms phase ids through hsdd-reconcile

options.label: guessed first phase ids
options.consequence: phase plans do not exist yet; every id would be a guess

chosen: node ids, provisional
why: Same reason as S06: no phase plan exists. consumers lists nidana.runtime (which also implements the live side), navigation, flutter, tooling and integration, as the root contract matrix does; external consumers are app topology modules and app topology tests.

question: Does this contract declare a typed topology identifier?

options.label: declare TopologyRef
options.consequence: the Spec §4.6 example and Guide C.5's v2 lint have a type to name; modules keep their references private

options.label: leave typed ids to modules
options.consequence: each module invents its own wrapper

chosen: declare TopologyRef
why: Spec §4.6 names TopologyRef in its Dart example and Guide C.5 lints exported TopologyRef values; a one-field value costs nothing.

question: S07 asks for two governance touches: add topology-dsl@v1 to ADR-003's affects (ADR-003 items 3 and 4 constrain its live guarantees G22 and G23), with ADR-001 item 4's wording 'live topology builder' aligned to the plan-interpretation path; and correct the root's OQ5 detail, which says server rewiring is 'covered by topology-dsl@v1's switchMap'. When do these run?

options.label: One touch step each, now
options.consequence: Each fix lands immediately, at the cost of interleaving small hsdd-adr and hsdd-spec steps between contract steps, and of re-touching the same ADRs again if later contracts raise similar links.

options.label: Batch after the last root contract
options.consequence: One hsdd-adr step after S14 fixes every ADR affects and Governed-by link and any ADR wording the nine contracts exposed; one root hsdd-spec touch fixes root prose. Until then the gate keeps reporting the links as warnings, and contract steps read the contracts, which already state the binding facts.

chosen: Batch after the last root contract
why: Neither touch blocks a contract step: S07's contract states the guarantees ADR-003 constrains, and S09 is told where the live binding goes. The next seven contracts are likely to expose more links of the same kind (bus-api@v1 and bus-testing@v1 against ADR-003, flutter-binding@v1 against ADR-001's binding rule), and one pass over them costs less than several. The signal that would change this: a contract step that misreads an ADR because of a missing link.

question: How does TransformEdge represent a pipeline of several stages, a write and a reduceInto, when Spec §6.5 sketches an edge with topic references at both ends?

options.label: Spec sketch literally
options.consequence: one edge per sink whose inputs are the upstream topics; a chain read, map, filter, write cannot be described, so the self-reference check of Spec §3.8 cannot inspect paths and the graph has no internal nodes

options.label: Edges over topic or stage inputs, sinks as edges
options.consequence: an edge's inputs are TopicInput (a read, with its dedup argument) or StageInput (an earlier edge); a write and a reduceInto are sink edges with an output topic; one list carries the whole DAG and keeps the Spec's field names; a write has no CombinatorKind, so combinator is nullable for writes; deviates from the Spec sketch

options.label: Separate sinks list
options.consequence: a sixth definition field for sinks; reduceInto, which has a CombinatorKind and is a sink, straddles both lists; analyses walk two structures

options.label: Sealed edge class per kind
options.consequence: exact typing per combinator, but eighteen or more classes that every consumer switches over and every new combinator breaks

chosen: Edges over topic or stage inputs, sinks as edges
why: Spec §3.8 and Guide C.1 define the intra-topology check as inspection of TopologyDefinition.transforms for paths from read to write through stateful operators, so the IR must carry the stage DAG; the Spec sketch cannot. One list with the Spec's field names is the smallest deviation, and CombinatorKind stays at the eighteen values topology-dsl@v1 fixed (a write is the edge with no combinator, validated by three named constructors). The edge also records the read's dedup argument and switchMap's retry reference, because Spec §3.9 makes any observable difference between two activations of one id an error and bus-api@v1 will most likely compare definitions. Signal that would have changed it: consumers that need typed per-kind access often, which would favor a sealed per-kind family.

question: OQ-M1: How does the recorder name a transformer (FunctionRef) in Dart?

options.label: Derive from toString, VM pattern only
options.consequence: FunctionRef.of reads the name between "from Function '" and the next quote; named on the VM and in AOT, stable obfuscated names under --obfuscate, anonymous on dart2js and dart2wasm and for closures; no DSL change; a static method loses its class

options.label: Derive with a dart2js fallback
options.consequence: names on web builds too, but dart2js names inline closures main_closure and minified builds minified:xx, so closures would get false names

options.label: Explicit name on each combinator
options.consequence: exact names everywhere at the cost of a name argument on every call; a change topology-dsl@v1 lists as not in v1

options.label: Optional explicit name, then derivation, then a positional placeholder
options.consequence: flexible, but placeholders make definition equality depend on stage position and need a topology-dsl@v1 amendment

options.label: Leave naming to the static catalog
options.consequence: definitions from buildDefinition() carry no names, so the runtime graph and the static graph differ, against Spec §6.5's single IR

chosen: Derive from toString, VM pattern only
why: The experiment shows JIT and AOT render the names of top-level functions, static methods (without class) and method tear-offs, obfuscated AOT renders stable obfuscated names, dart2js renders compiler-internal names even for inline closures, and dart2wasm renders none. The catalog and the CI checks, which are where names are read, run on the VM; Spec §6.2 makes transformers named standalone functions; topology-dsl@v1's Versioning already answers OQ-M1 by derivation here. Equality is by name, so recording one declaration twice gives equal definitions even with inline closures (topology-dsl@v1 G9). Signal that would have changed it: a v1 consumer needing names in web builds, or static methods of one name in different classes colliding in practice; either brings an optional explicit name as a compatible topology-dsl@v1 addition.

question: Does the IR carry the durations of debounce, delay, sample and buffer, or does the self-reference analysis treat them as not mediating?

options.label: Carry durations
options.consequence: isStateBearing holds for those four with a positive duration, as topology-dsl@v1's Self-reference column states; graph labels and definition equality see durations

options.label: Treat them as not mediating
options.consequence: a smaller IR, but a debounce feedback loop that Spec §3.8 allows (a stateful chain that cannot loop back in zero time) would be rejected, and topology-dsl@v1's table would need an amendment

chosen: Carry durations
why: topology-dsl@v1 already marks the four stages as mediating when the duration is positive, and Spec §3.8 accepts a stateful chain that cannot loop back in zero time; carrying the duration decides the rule from the IR alone and costs one optional field. A zero duration does not mediate, which the findings sample exercises.

question: Which public library carries the IR, the graphs, the renderers, the JSON codec and the analyses?

options.label: All in the main library
options.consequence: one import for every consumer; every topology module's namespace also carries renderer, codec and analysis names such as JsonRenderer

options.label: Value types in the main library, the rest in topology_ir.dart
options.consequence: buildDefinition(), which modules call, returns types the main library has; the runtime, tooling and tests import a second library; module namespaces stay small

options.label: Everything in topology_ir.dart
options.consequence: impossible without changing topology-dsl@v1, whose surface fixture uses TopologyDefinition through the main library alone

chosen: Value types in the main library, the rest in topology_ir.dart
why: topology-dsl@v1's surface fixture reads TopologyDefinition from the main library, so the value types must be there; nothing in a topology module needs a renderer or an analysis. ADR-002 item 3 lets the declaring contract name a second public library. The case is close: the signal that would have changed it is app topology tests that routinely render graphs, which would favor one library.

question: Does a definition take reads and writes as arguments, or derive them from its edges?

options.label: Derive them
options.consequence: the constructor takes id, scope and edges; an inconsistent definition cannot exist; the JSON form still lists reads and writes for CI tools, and the decoder rejects a document whose lists disagree with its edges

options.label: Take them as arguments
options.consequence: matches the Spec sketch's five constructor fields and eases hand-built test definitions, but a definition can then contradict its own edges

chosen: Derive them
why: A pure core should make the inconsistent value unrepresentable; tests build definitions by recording topologies, which yields consistent edges anyway. The redundant lists stay in the JSON form, where CI tools that need only reads and writes per topology (cycles, orphans) read them without walking edges.
evidence: Guide C.3 (topology-graph.json for cycle detection and orphan analysis)

question: How does a shell publisher's claim and its scope enter the scope-compatibility and single-writer analyses without this contract naming a bus type?

options.label: ShellClaim values inside TopologyGraph
options.consequence: a claim is (MessageSource source, Scope scope defaulting to application, Set<TopicRef> state topics); the graph holds topologies and claims; bus.toGraph() and the catalog build the same type; claims appear as source nodes in renderings, as Spec §3.11 describes

options.label: A separate ownership argument to each analysis
options.consequence: graphs stay topology-only, but every analysis grows a parameter, renderings cannot show shell writers, and the static and live views diverge

options.label: Model claims as pseudo-topologies
options.consequence: no new type, but a claim has no edges or reads, its source is not a topology id, and cycle and self-reference analyses would have to skip them

chosen: ShellClaim values inside TopologyGraph
why: Spec §3.11 has publisher claims appear as source nodes in the topology graph and Spec §7.2 gives each claimant a scope, application when unbound; one value with those three parts carries exactly that. Writers are identified by MessageSource, the identity their publishes already carry (TopologySource for a topology), so findings name the current owner as Spec §3.11 requires. A claim rejects topology and unknown sources, an empty set and non-state topics, since only state topics are claimed (Spec §2.4).

question: What does a graph do with two definitions of one topologyId, and with two equal claims?

options.label: Collapse equal definitions, reject unequal ones, keep equal claims
options.consequence: a graph is a map from id to definition, as Spec §3.9 makes the bus; two publishers with one source and one write set stay two claimants, so the single-writer check sees both; the catalog must report duplicate ids before building a graph

options.label: Keep every definition and report duplicates as a finding
options.consequence: the catalog gets a diagnostic for free, but every analysis keyed by topology id becomes ambiguous and the check is not in root D1's v1 list

options.label: Collapse equal claims too
options.consequence: set semantics throughout, but two identical publisher constructions, a real runtime first-claim failure, would pass the static single-writer check

chosen: Collapse equal definitions, reject unequal ones, keep equal claims
why: Spec §3.9: activating one id twice with the same declaration is the same topology, with a different one an error, so the graph mirrors the bus. Spec §3.11's runtime first-claim rejects a second publisher even when it is identical to the first, so the static view must count it. Signal that would have changed it: catalogs that legitimately hold one id in two coordination domains.

question: What shape do the analyses take: what they consume, what they return, and which checks are here?

options.label: One function per analysis over TopologyGraph, typed findings in a sealed family, plus analyzeTopologyGraph
options.consequence: cycles, self-references, writer conflicts and scope violations as final classes under sealed TopologyFinding, a fixed result order, topic name collisions over caller-supplied TopicDeclaration values; the runtime and the workspace scan call the same functions

options.label: Methods on TopologyGraph returning strings
options.consequence: compact, but untyped diagnostics that bus-api@v1 and nidana-checks@v1 would each parse

options.label: Leave single-writer to the runtime and the scan
options.consequence: matches nidana.model's Owns list literally, but ADR-002 item 8 has the scan run single-writer by calling the contracts package's analyses, the functions activation also calls

chosen: One function per analysis over TopologyGraph, typed findings in a sealed family, plus analyzeTopologyGraph
why: Root D4 and ADR-002 item 8 require activation and CI to run the same pure functions; typed sealed findings let both hosts map them to diagnostics exhaustively. Single-writer is included because ADR-002 item 8 lists it among the analyses the scan calls; nidana.model's Owns list should name it (note for the orchestrator). The guarantee that a finding-free graph stays finding-free when topologies or claims are removed (G17) lets the bus keep its active set clean by rejecting any activation or publisher whose graph has a finding.

question: What exactly is an unmediated self-read, and what does a SelfReference finding report?

options.label: Paths of non-state-bearing edges from a read to a write of the topic, every edge on them reported
options.consequence: well defined whatever the algorithm (forward reach from the read intersected with backward reach from the write); a withLatestFrom over the topology's own state is unmediated, as topology-dsl@v1's column marks it

options.label: Report one representative path
options.consequence: a shorter diagnostic, but which path is algorithm-dependent and untestable as a value

options.label: Treat a latest input of withLatestFrom as mediating
options.consequence: accepts the reducer-by-withLatestFrom pattern, which cannot loop in zero time, but contradicts topology-dsl@v1's Self-reference column and the reduceInto idiom Spec §6.3 provides

chosen: Paths of non-state-bearing edges from a read to a write of the topic, every edge on them reported
why: Spec §3.8 asks that any read of a self-written topic reach the write only through a state-bearing operator; the set of edges on unmediated paths is unique, so the finding is a value the fixtures can pin. topology-dsl@v1 fixed which stages mediate, and reduceInto is the DSL's reducer. Signal that would have changed it: real topologies that need withLatestFrom over their own state.

question: What counts as a topic name collision (Spec §4.3)?

options.label: Any two distinct declarations of one name
options.consequence: two registries declaring cart.items fail CI even with one type; the input carries a caller-chosen site so equal declarations from two places stay distinct

options.label: Only declarations whose variant or type differ
options.consequence: mirrors the runtime check, but two teams silently sharing a channel by accident would pass
