options.consequence: claim, observe, planning, BackTo synthesis, paired writes, timestamps, diagnostics and disposal written once; a platform implements four stack calls, its stack and its confirmations; flutter-binding@v1's FlutterNavigationExecutor is a Flutter router with wiring, not a subclass

options.label: an abstract base executor each platform subclasses
options.consequence: the Guide's FlutterNavigationExecutor-is-a-NavigationExecutor shape; template-method inheritance the owner's composition preference disfavors

options.label: an interface only; each platform writes the whole executor
options.consequence: Guide §3.4 literally; every platform reimplements the bus logic, and the suite tests each copy

chosen: a final NavigationExecutor in this package over a NavigationRouter port the platform implements
why: nidana.navigation's spec already owns the bus-facing duties (claim, paired writes, BackTo synthesis) and nidana.flutter's spec owns only the implementation against its router, so the split follows the node specs; composition over inheritance per the owner. Node set and contract set unchanged, so not a tree-shape stop.

question: What does each intent do to the stack (the Specification is silent; Guide §3.4 maps GoTo to go_router's location-based go)?

options.label: GoTo pushes; Replace replaces the top; Back pops; BackTo pops to the topmost entry of its route; ShowModal pushes modal; DismissModal pops a modal
options.consequence: one meaning every router can realize, so one suite checks every platform; BackTo and Replace stay distinct; no reset-the-stack intent in v1; flutter-binding must map GoTo to push

options.label: GoTo resets the stack to the route (go semantics)
options.consequence: matches the Guide's go_router mapping on flat routes; stack contents depend on the router's route tree; Back after GoTo is usually at the root, which leaves BackTo nearly useless

chosen: GoTo pushes; Replace replaces the top; Back pops; BackTo pops to the topmost entry of its route; ShowModal pushes modal; DismissModal pops a modal
why: A portable conformance suite needs one stack meaning, and BackTo's presence in the vocabulary implies stacks grown by GoTo. Close call against go semantics; the signal that would change it is an owner preference for URL-location navigation on web, which would add a reset intent rather than redefine GoTo.

question: What does the executor do with an intent the stack does not admit (Back at the root, BackTo a route not on the stack, DismissModal with no modal on top)?

options.label: refuse: nothing navigates or is written; dev mode reports NavigationRefused
options.consequence: uniform across routers; a Flutter pop of the last route cannot happen through intents

options.label: pass the call to the platform
options.consequence: router-defined results, such as an empty Navigator

chosen: refuse: nothing navigates or is written; dev mode reports NavigationRefused
why: Keeps behavior the same on every router and the suite router-neutral; uses bus-api@v1's ShellDiagnostic extension point (root D8). The diagnostic holds the reason and BackTo's route, never arguments (bus-api@v1 G4). BackTo to the route already on top is a no-op, not a refusal.

question: How does a router report transitions, and how many history entries does a synthesized BackTo produce?

options.label: one perform per intent, validated before acting, confirmed once with the stack it left and the intent; platform transitions confirmed with const Back()
options.consequence: a synthesized BackTo (k pops) and a native popUntil both yield one transition; routers must suppress their own observer events during a perform

options.label: one confirmation per platform pop
options.consequence: a synthesized BackTo writes k transitions and a native popUntil also k (Flutter observers see each pop), so history differs from the intent stream

chosen: one perform per intent, validated before acting, confirmed once with the stack it left and the intent; platform transitions confirmed with const Back()
why: Guide §3.4 requires history and currentRoute to agree and the intent to come from the platform's confirmation; one transition per intent makes BackTo identical whether native or synthesized, which the VM binding checks by running every case on both capabilities. The stand-in Flutter router shows the suppression is small.

question: Does the executor write the router's initial route at construction, and does it report a construction after start()?

options.label: write the initial top to nav.current-route (no history entry) and report LateExecutorConstruction in dev mode
options.consequence: nav.current-route is truthful from start(); the bootstrap mistake that loses a queued deep link is visible

options.label: leave RouteState.initial until the first navigation, no diagnostic
options.consequence: less code; nav.current-route reads NavRoute.none until the user navigates

chosen: write the initial top to nav.current-route (no history entry) and report LateExecutorConstruction in dev mode
why: Guide §3.5 makes construction before start() part of the bootstrap order; bus-api@v1's LateApplicationActivation is the analogous runtime diagnostic. No history entry because no transition was confirmed.

question: Whether this contract declares the in-memory router publicly, and where its binding lives.

options.label: public InMemoryRouter in package:nidana_dart_navigation/testing.dart; its binding in this contract's fixture directory
options.consequence: apps and nidana.integration get a VM router for navigation tests without Flutter; ADR-001 item 4 puts the binding here because this Interface declares it

options.label: a private stand-in inside the fixtures only
options.consequence: no public test double; every consumer writes its own, each needing its own binding (ADR-001 item 11)

options.label: in the main library
options.consequence: test infrastructure in the production import

chosen: public InMemoryRouter in package:nidana_dart_navigation/testing.dart; its binding in this contract's fixture directory
why: Mirrors the runtime's testing.dart (ADR-002 item 3: other public libraries named by their contract); nidana.navigation's isolation strategy already names an in-memory router; G26 keeps testing.dart free of test and flutter_test imports.

question: How are the conformance cases split between libraries and bindings?

options.label: two libraries: a VM-only navigation suite on TestBus (one implementation) and a runner-neutral executor suite (one per platform), the VM binding registering each executor case on both pop-until capabilities
options.consequence: resolver cases can assert with TestBus, stub, input and recorder literals; the executor harness names no bus-testing type; synthesized BackTo runs end to end on the VM

options.label: one library with a harness abstracting the bus for everything
options.consequence: resolver cases lose TestBus's deterministic recorder and must run under testWidgets too

chosen: two libraries: a VM-only navigation suite on TestBus (one implementation) and a runner-neutral executor suite (one per platform), the VM binding registering each executor case on both pop-until capabilities
why: bus-testing@v1's note: resolver tests run on a TestBus, while the executor harness must not name TestBus or settle; topology-dsl@v1's recording and live split is the precedent. The second registration keeps the guarantee-id prefix so --guarantee selects both (T8 in the experiment).

question: Is the app's deep-link mapping total or may it return nothing?

options.label: total: DeepLinkResolver returns a ResolvedNavIntent
options.consequence: every intent yields exactly one resolved intent; an unknown link maps to a route the app chooses

options.label: nullable: null drops the link
options.consequence: silent drops; one more filter stage in the template

chosen: total: DeepLinkResolver returns a ResolvedNavIntent
why: Keeps G14's one-to-one mapping and makes unknown links observable as navigations (Guide §3.1 'unobservable transitions'). Signal: an app that must ignore unknown links silently.

question: Does the contract pin the resolver template's stages and ids, and the access-requirement spelling?

options.label: pin id nav-resolver, APPLICATION scope, reads, writes and the stage order; requirement variants PublicAccess, AuthenticatedAccess, RoleAccess, CustomAccess with a fallback on the policy
options.consequence: the IR (Spec §6.5) shows resolve-before-guard and is checkable; equal configurations record equal definitions (idempotent activation); names do not collide with app ADT variants such as AuthState.Authenticated

options.label: pin only reads and writes; variants named Public, Authenticated, Role, Custom
options.consequence: freer implementation; the ordering fix is not visible in the IR; Authenticated collides with the Guide's own AuthState.Authenticated in an app that imports both

chosen: pin id nav-resolver, APPLICATION scope, reads, writes and the stage order; requirement variants PublicAccess, AuthenticatedAccess, RoleAccess, CustomAccess with a fallback on the policy
why: Guide §3.4 fixes the id and scope; pinning the stages makes Refinement 3 checkable from the recorded IR. The fallback lets an app close unlisted routes. No experiment for the variant collision beyond the Guide's naming.

question: How does the contract own result handling (Guide §3.6)?

options.label: a resultsFor helper over the topology DSL (withLatestFrom, filter, map) plus the stated pattern
options.consequence: the Guide's pattern once, recordable and testable; matching on payloads only

options.label: pattern only, no declaration
options.consequence: nothing to test; each app rewrites the three stages

chosen: a resultsFor helper over the topology DSL (withLatestFrom, filter, map) plus the stated pattern
why: nidana.navigation's Owns list includes result handling; a helper gives G16 a target. No evidence that apps need more.

question: Names and defaults: executor default name, resolver id, history buffer, testing library name.

options.label: ExecutorSource('navigation') by default; resolver id 'nav-resolver', not configurable; nav.history buffer 20; testing.dart
options.consequence: Guide §3.3 and §3.4 values; Flutter passes its own name such as 'flutter-navigation'; one resolver per bus

options.label: name required, id configurable
options.consequence: more ceremony at every construction; two resolvers on one bus would race on nav.resolved-intent anyway

chosen: ExecutorSource('navigation') by default; resolver id 'nav-resolver', not configurable; nav.history buffer 20; testing.dart
why: Guide values where it gives them; no evidence otherwise.

question: The S11 stand-in runtime delivers an activation's connection one microtask after activate, so a deep link queued before start() reaches the resolver's withLatestFrom before its auth read has a value and is dropped. Do the fixtures pin the real bootstrap (activate; start; with nothing between) or let microtasks run between activation and start()?

options.label: pin the real bootstrap and read bus-api@v1 G22 with G34 as requiring the connection before the queue (Refinement 8)
options.consequence: G14 and G24 fail against a runtime that does not deliver the connection first; bus-api@v1 needs its statement and fixtures sharpened; the experiment's runtime copy carries the change and still passes every bus-api@v1 and bus-testing@v1 case

options.label: flush between activation and start() in the cases
options.consequence: passes on the S11 stand-in, but tests a bootstrap no app writes (Guide §3.5 calls start() right after activation), so a real deep-link drop would pass the gate

chosen: pin the real bootstrap and read bus-api@v1 G22 with G34 as requiring the connection before the queue (Refinement 8)
why: Spec §3.13 and Guide §3.5 promise that a deep link published before start() is delivered once the resolver is subscribed; bus-api@v1 G22 already says the connection reaches reads before later values, but no bus-api case pins it and its G34 case flushes before start(). The probe shows the drop on the S11 runtime and the fix keeping bus-api's 86, 43 and bus-testing's 45 cases green. Under testWidgets the drop is hidden because pumpWidget runs the microtask before start().

question: bus-api@v1's publish<T>(MultiWriterTopic<T>, T) widens T, so publishing a DeepLink to nav.resolved-intent compiles. Does this contract carry a reject line for it now?

options.label: state G1 for this contract's own declarations and record the gap (Refinement 9)
options.consequence: every navigation-api fixture passes against bus-api@v1 as written; the publish hole is closed by an amendment of bus-api@v1, after which a reject line can be added here compatibly

options.label: add a reject line expecting could_not_infer now
options.consequence: the line fails until bus-api@v1 is amended, so nidana.navigation's gate would depend on another contract's pending change

chosen: state G1 for this contract's own declarations and record the gap (Refinement 9)
why: The probe shows W1 and W2 compile today and that the bounded form publish<T, V extends T> rejects both with could_not_infer while accepting well-typed publishes (W5); at run time the stand-in throws TypeError at delivery. The gap violates Spec §4.2 for every topic, so it belongs to bus-api@v1.

question: Seeded defects survived (from read off the bus, argsOf with a same-typed other route, query-parameter equality). Add cases or accept the gaps?

options.label: add the three assertions
options.consequence: G21 gains a case for confirmations made inside one delivery chain; G5 and G8 cases tighten

options.label: accept
options.consequence: an executor that reads from via getCurrentValue, and two equality defects, would pass the suite

chosen: add the three assertions
why: Each was a real defect the suite let through in the experiment's mutation runs.

question: S12 asks for a bus-api@v1 amendment: (a) a topology activated before start() is connected to its reads before start() delivers the queue, with cases that catch a runtime dropping a queued deep link (the S11 stand-in passes every current case and still drops it); (b) Bus.publish and Publisher.publish become publish<T, V extends T>(MultiWriterTopic<T> topic, V value), so publishing a String to an EventTopic<int>, or a DeepLink to nav.resolved-intent, no longer compiles. S11 asked for two wording fixes to the same contract. When does the amendment run, and is (b) a breaking amendment that stops the run?

options.label: Amend bus-api@v1 now, before flutter-binding@v1, all four changes in one step
options.consequence: flutter-binding@v1 is authored against the corrected bootstrap guarantee it depends on; the root contracts after it shift by one step; the batched wording fixes leave the post-S15 touch-up list.

options.label: Batch into the post-S15 touch-up
options.consequence: flutter-binding@v1 would bind its executor suite against a bus-api@v1 whose bootstrap guarantee is known to be too weak, and might encode the workaround S12 found (mount first, start after the first frame) as its own guarantee.

options.label: Treat (b) as breaking and stop
options.consequence: The owner decides a signature change that touches only bus-api@v1's own fixtures.

chosen: Amend bus-api@v1 now, before flutter-binding@v1, all four changes in one step
why: Change (a) is a missing guarantee that the next contract depends on, so it must land first. Change (b) is a signature change, but the stop condition is an amendment that would break an existing consumer, and none exists: no code, every contract draft, and a search of every fixture under hsdd/contract/fixture/ finds explicit type arguments to publish only in bus-api@v1's own surface and reject files, which the amendment rewrites (the other matches declare harness methods). It restores Spec §4.2 (writing a value of the wrong type to a typed topic is a compile error). One step for all four changes keeps bus-api@v1 touched once.

question: Change (b): which signature makes a value of the wrong type a compile error without changing any fixture outside bus-api@v1? The orchestrator named publish<T, V extends T>(MultiWriterTopic<T> topic, V value).

options.label: publish<T, V extends T>, as named
options.consequence: Rejects a wrong value type with could_not_infer, but a state topic passed to publish now leaves T uninferred (dynamic) and the analyzer adds inference_failure_on_function_invocation under strict-inference; navigation-api@v1's reject/current_route_is_claimed_by_the_executor.dart then fails on lines 10 and 12, so a fixture outside bus-api@v1 would have to change: a run-stop-candidate under this step's rule (experiment T10, probe P2 line 27).

options.label: publish<T extends Object?, V extends T>
options.consequence: The same type relation (Object? is an unbounded parameter's bound already); only a failed inference falls back to Object? instead of dynamic, so a state topic reports argument_type_not_assignable alone. Wrong value types are rejected identically (could_not_infer); every fixture outside bus-api@v1 passes unchanged (T3, T7).

options.label: keep publish<T>(MultiWriterTopic<T>, T) and drop (b)
options.consequence: No fixture changes, but Spec §4.2's compile-time typing stays unmet: publish(EventTopic<int>, 'one') and a DeepLink to nav.resolved-intent compile and fail at run time (navigation-api@v1 Refinement 9).

chosen: publish<T extends Object?, V extends T>
why: It meets (b)'s purpose exactly and is the only one of the three that satisfies both (b) and the step's compatibility rule. The prescribed spelling differs only in the implicit bound, and that difference is what produces the extra strict-inference warning. Found by experiment, not by the orchestrator's search for explicit type arguments, which was correct as far as it went (only bus-api@v1's own surface/bus.dart and no_publisherless_state_publish.dart pass explicit type arguments) but missed that a reject fixture pins the full diagnostic set of a line. Signal that would have changed my mind: a lint in package:lints/recommended flagging the redundant bound (T0 shows none fires) or the orchestrator treating the spelled-out bound as a different change from the one it authorized, in which case the named form is a run-stop-candidate with the T10 evidence.

question: Change (a): is the connection rule a sharpening of G22 and G34 or a new guarantee after G39?

options.label: sharpen G22, G34 and the connection rule
options.consequence: Keeps the ids navigation-api@v1 already cites (Refinement 8, G24 rest on bus-api@v1 G22 and G34); the earlier G22 already said the connection reaches the reads before any value published after activate returns, so the rule is a restatement in terms of deliveries, not a new property.

options.label: new G40 for the connection rule
options.consequence: A separate id to cite, but splits one activation rule across G22 and G40 and leaves navigation-api@v1's citations pointing at the weaker statement.

chosen: sharpen G22, G34 and the connection rule
why: The earlier G22, G34 and Spec §3.13 ('no APPLICATION topology can miss an event that was published before it subscribed') already intended it; only the fixtures failed to pin it. ADR-001 item 3 is respected: no id is renumbered or reused.

question: Does G22 pin that the publishes a connection causes are made from a provider-zone microtask, never within activate, as S12 asked, or keep only 'delivered once the microtasks queued during activate have run'?

options.label: pin the deferral, with a case
options.consequence: A runtime that delivers connection outputs inside activate fails; a topology activated right after another (in a module acquire, or a bootstrap) receives the first one's connection outputs.

options.label: leave the earlier wording
options.consequence: Admits a runtime that delivers connection outputs synchronously inside activate, which the earlier wording also satisfied literally.

chosen: pin the deferral, with a case
why: Seeded defect T10 (connection publishes made within activate) fails the new G22 case and the existing 'G34 ... the order of the activations before start does not change what is delivered' case, so the deferral is what makes activation order irrelevant; the navigation-api-fixtures runtime already behaves this way and every consumer suite passes on it.

question: How do the new (a) cases detect a late connection?

options.label: a withLatestFrom gate over a state read
options.consequence: Drops a primary value that arrives before the read's first value, so a late connection shows as a missing output; the same shape as navigation-api@v1's nav-resolver, so the cases model the deep-link bootstrap.

options.label: a combineLatest or a recorder-order check
options.consequence: combineLatest emits late rather than dropping, which a flush hides; an order check over envelopes cannot see when a read received its first value, since the connection is not a publish.

chosen: a withLatestFrom gate over a state read
why: It turns the timing question into a value difference the harness can assert synchronously, and S12's connection probe already showed it separates the S11 runtime from a correct one.

question: Change (b): extend G11 and G19 with the value-type rule, or add a guarantee?

options.label: new G40 with its own reject library
options.consequence: One rule over both publish paths, as topology-dsl@v1 G3 states it for write; ADR-001 item 4 wants one reject library per type-level guarantee, so publish_value_matches_topic.dart covers G40 alone.

options.label: extend G11 and G19
options.consequence: No new id, but one rule stated twice and the reject lines split across two files whose guarantees are about the topic variant, not the value.

chosen: new G40 with its own reject library
why: The value-type rule is distinct from the variant rule G11 and G19 state; a separate id lets phase gates restrict by it. Every reject code was confirmed (T3, T4).

question: Explicit type arguments can still widen T through Dart's covariant generics (publish<num, double> on an EventTopic<int> compiles, probe P16, P26). What does G40 say about them?

options.label: state the limit in G40
options.consequence: The guarantee is exact about what it covers (inferred type arguments); no runtime behavior is promised for the widened call.

options.label: add a run-time guarantee (a throw) with a behavior case
options.consequence: Closes the hole at run time, but adds a check on every publish path and a rule no consumer asked for.

options.label: say nothing
options.consequence: G40 would read as if every wrong value were a compile error, which is false.

chosen: state the limit in G40
why: No evidence that anyone writes explicit widening type arguments; stating the limit keeps the guarantee honest. A static check (nidana-checks@v1) is the cheaper closure if it ever matters. Signal that would change it: a consumer contract or app pattern that forwards topics through explicitly widened generics.

question: Change (c): how does G38 admit the settle operation's real event-loop turns?

options.label: except them in G38, citing bus-testing@v1 G12 and ADR-003 item 6
options.consequence: G38 and bus-testing@v1 G12, G20 state the same exception; G38 stays a source property checked by nidana.runtime's gates.

options.label: leave G38 and rely on bus-testing@v1's statement
options.consequence: The two contracts contradict each other on one package's sources.

chosen: except them in G38, citing bus-testing@v1 G12 and ADR-003 item 6
why: ADR-003 item 6 is accepted and requires the real turns; S11 asked for exactly this clarification. No consumer relies on G38.

question: Change (d): how does the delivery rule name the recorders?

options.label: the recorders attached to the bus first, in attachment order (bus-testing@v1 G14, G17)
options.consequence: Matches bus-testing@v1's EnvelopeRecorder.attach on any bus, a widget test's production-provider bus included; Refinement 4 says the same.

options.label: keep 'the recorder of a TestBus'
options.consequence: Contradicts bus-testing@v1 G14 and G17 for a recorder attached to a production-provider bus.

chosen: the recorders attached to the bus first, in attachment order (bus-testing@v1 G14, G17)
why: Editorial alignment S11 asked for; bus-testing@v1 already states the behavior, and no fixture changes.

question: After the connection, does every later delivery reach a topology's read during that delivery, so the deliveries start() makes reach a topology's reads in queue order across topics? The navigation-api-fixtures runtime, which S12 offered as making (a) hold, connects synchronously but holds back the deliveries made before the RxDart replay's first microtask, so a state publish queued between two queued events reaches a withLatestFrom read after the second event (T10: [41, 51] where [41, 57] is the queue order).

options.label: pin it: a connected read receives each later delivery during that delivery
options.consequence: A restored state queued before start (an auth session written by a service) reaches the nav-resolver's read before a deep link queued after it; the runtime needs a synchronous, non-replaying path for topology reads (the stand-in uses a sync broadcast controller per cell); every consumer suite passes on it (T7). Goes beyond Spec §3.3's general position that cross-topic ordering is not guaranteed, for synchronous deliveries on one bus.

options.label: pin only that the connection precedes the queue
options.consequence: What S12 asked for literally; the navigation-api-fixtures runtime suffices, but a queued state publish can reach a topology after a later-queued event, so the deep-link guard can see the initial auth state instead of the restored one.

chosen: pin it: a connected read receives each later delivery during that delivery
why: The delivery rule already says a delivery runs synchronously and hands the envelope to the subscriptions, and G34 says start() delivers the queue in order; a read the connection reached is an established subscriber, and only RxDart's replay buffering made the window. Spec §3.13 makes the barrier the deep-link mechanism, which only works if the queue reaches the resolver in order. Medium confidence because it strengthens cross-topic ordering at a topology beyond Spec §3.3's portable minimum. Signal that would change it: nidana.runtime's design finding that a non-replaying read path costs more than the guarantee is worth, or the owner preferring Spec §3.3's weaker stance for portability.

question: Is this amendment within v1, given that the Breaking list names retyping a declaration and changing a delivery rule?

options.label: within v1, with a Versioning line
options.consequence: No consumer contract changes; the line records the four changes, why each is compatible here, and the experiment that shows every other contract's fixtures pass unchanged.

options.label: draft bus-api@v2
options.consequence: A v2 and migration note for a draft contract with no producer or consumer code, and every consumer contract re-pointed.

chosen: within v1, with a Versioning line
why: The orchestrator's rule, verified: no package exists and an amendment breaks a consumer only by breaking another contract's fixtures; T1 to T7 replay every fixture of topology-dsl@v1 (live suite), bus-testing@v1 and navigation-api@v1 unchanged and passing. (a) restates what the earlier wording and Spec §3.13 intended; (b) rejects only calls that were wrong at run time and calls with one explicit type argument, which only bus-api@v1's own fixtures made. Timestamp taken just after the line was written (the contract's last edit is 19:46:33Z).

question: The Validation section said the fixtures assume topic-model@v1 declares MultiWriterTopic. Keep the assumption or cite the declaration?

options.label: cite topic-model@v1 G27 and docs/auto-run/experiments/topic-model-multi-writer/
options.consequence: States a fact instead of an assumption, as S10 suggested.

options.label: keep the assumption
options.consequence: Stale since S10.

chosen: cite topic-model@v1 G27 and docs/auto-run/experiments/topic-model-multi-writer/
why: topic-model@v1 declares MultiWriterTopic since S10 (its G27), and that experiment replays this contract's surface and reject sets with and without it.

question: S13 declared publish<T extends Object?, V extends T>(MultiWriterTopic<T>, V) instead of the publish<T, V extends T> the orchestrator named, because the named form makes a failed inference fall back to dynamic, which adds inference_failure_on_function_invocation under strict-inference and breaks navigation-api@v1's reject/current_route_is_claimed_by_the_executor.dart (experiment T10). Is the written-out bound a different change from the one authorized, making this a run-stop?

options.label: Same change; accept
options.consequence: The amendment stands: wrong value types do not compile, a state topic still reports argument_type_not_assignable alone, and no fixture outside bus-api@v1 changes.

options.label: Different change; treat the named form as a breaking amendment and stop
options.consequence: The owner decides between two spellings of one signature, one of which breaks a consumer fixture and one of which does not.

chosen: Same change; accept
why: The authorization was for the change's effect: restore Spec §4.2's compile-time type check on publish without breaking any other contract's fixtures. The written-out bound has the same subtyping relation and is the only spelling that meets the second condition; experiment T10 shows the named spelling would have broken navigation-api@v1. The breaking-amend stop guards existing consumers, and the accepted form breaks none.

question: OQ-F1: which router do the Flutter executor and the module binding target: Flutter's own Navigator and Router APIs, or go_router as Guide §3.4 shows, and does that router become a dependency of the adapter?

options.label: Flutter Navigator, no router dependency
options.consequence: The adapter depends on Flutter alone; the router keeps its own stack, applies performs synchronously and confirms before perform returns; apps on go_router implement navigation-api@v1's NavigationRouter themselves; no web URL sync in v1.

options.label: go_router as a dependency
options.consequence: Matches Guide §3.4's example and gives URL routing, but the published adapter would carry material_ui, cupertino_ui, flutter_localizations and intl; push lands a frame later, there is no pop-until, go has route-tree semantics that contradict navigation-api@v1 Refinement 7, and go_router handles the platform's initial route itself, past the bus guard.

options.label: Navigator now, plus a go_router NavigationRouter package in v1
options.consequence: Serves both kinds of app, but adds a package and a node-level deliverable root D1 does not schedule.

chosen: Flutter Navigator, no router dependency
why: The experiment settled the facts: Navigator calls reach observers synchronously (P2), so a router over Navigator can meet navigation-api@v1 G18 exactly (26 of 26 executor cases under testWidgets); go_router's push reaches the Navigator only after a frame (R2), it has no popUntil (R3), it navigates to the platform's initial route by itself (R4), go turns [/, /a] into [/, /b] (R5), and 18.x pulls material and cupertino packages (R1). navigation-api@v1 Refinement 7 already rejected go's semantics for GoTo, and ADR-002 adds a router package only if this question selects one. Not a tree-shape stop: both options produce the same nodes and the same contract set. The signal that would have changed my mind: an owner-named v1 app that needs web URL synchronization or is already on go_router.

question: Settle the bootstrap: NavigationExecutor reads router.stack when constructed, so either the Navigator is mounted first, or the router accepts calls before mount.

options.label: Router accepts performs before mount
options.consequence: Guide §3.5's order (resolver, executor, start(), runApp) works unchanged; the router keeps its stack and the hosting Navigator starts from it.

options.label: Navigator mounted before the executor is constructed
options.consequence: The executor and start() must wait for the first frame; a deep link queued before start() needs the bootstrap to defer start() into a post-frame callback.

chosen: Router accepts performs before mount
why: runApp attaches the root widget from a Timer, so the microtasks in which start()'s reentrant deliveries reach the executor run while no Navigator exists (P1); the second option would reorder Guide §3.5's bootstrap for every app. G12 and G16 state and test it.

question: Which routes hold a module scope reference: every route on the Navigator's stack whose path matches, or only the visible top route?

options.label: Stack membership
options.consequence: A module stays active while any of its routes is on the stack, covered or not; its covered pages keep their module-owned state alive.

options.label: Top route only
options.consequence: A module is released when another module's route covers it, and reactivated on return; covered pages, still mounted, read state whose owner is gone.

chosen: Stack membership
why: Flutter keeps covered routes mounted (P3), so their PAGE topologies stay active, and Spec §7.2 requires a state topic's owner to live at least as long as its readers. Spec §7.3 says module scope ends when navigation leaves the subtree and is silent on stacked navigators, so the reading is a clarification worth upstreaming. The signal that would have changed my mind: an owner requirement to tear down covered modules for memory.

question: When is a popped route's module reference released: at didPop, or when the route is disposed after its exit transition?

options.label: At didPop
options.consequence: Follows Spec §7.3's push and pop binding; the grace period covers the exit transition.

options.label: At route disposal
options.consequence: Tracks the page's real lifetime, but NavigatorObserver has no disposal callback, so it needs per-route hooks the app's route builder would have to install.

chosen: At didPop
why: Spec §7.3 binds the reference to route push and pop and makes the grace period configurable for slow transition animations; P6 shows observers get no disposal notice.

question: On a route replacement inside a module's subtree, in which order are references acquired and released?

options.label: Acquire new, then release old
options.consequence: The count never crosses zero, so even a zero grace period keeps the topologies.

options.label: Release old, then acquire new
options.consequence: With a zero grace period the topologies tear down and reactivate on every in-subtree replace.

chosen: Acquire new, then release old
why: Spec §7.3 item 2: an in-subtree navigation balances the count without crossing zero. P2 shows pushReplacement reports didReplace, so the observer sees both routes in one callback.

question: What does the module observer do when an acquire throws (bus-api@v1 G28 rethrows an activation failure)?

options.label: Report through FlutterError.reportError
options.consequence: The error surfaces in debug runs and tests (takeException); the route holds no reference; the Navigator keeps working.

options.label: Rethrow into the Navigator
options.consequence: The exception escapes the Navigator's observer notification and leaves the Navigator locked: later operations fail the '!_debugLocked' assertion.

chosen: Report through FlutterError.reportError
why: Found by experiment: the first version of the suite threw ActivationRejected from didPush, and the Navigator then failed '!_debugLocked' assertions at unmount. Reporting matches how Flutter itself reports observer errors.

question: Two mounted PageScopes that name one topology id (one route pushed twice): how is the shared handle released?

options.label: Count holders per bus and topology id
options.consequence: The topology lives until the last mounted scope naming it unmounts.

options.label: Activate and deactivate per mount
options.consequence: The first unmount deactivates the shared handle (bus-api@v1 G25) and the page below loses its topology.

options.label: Reject a second mount
options.consequence: A route pushed twice fails to mount.

chosen: Count holders per bus and topology id
why: Activation is idempotent and returns one handle (Spec §3.9, bus-api@v1 G23), whose deactivation ends the topology for every holder (G25). Spec §7.3's React StrictMode note asks adapters to offset a duplicate mount the same way for modules; Spec §7.1 is silent for pages, so it is marked for upstreaming. A bus-api@v1 'page scope' primitive would move the count into the runtime; not needed for v1.

question: Does a PageScope rebind when rebuilt with other arguments (route, topologies, writes)?

options.label: Bind once, at mount
options.consequence: Simple and ordering-free; a new key remounts it.

options.label: Rebind on change
options.consequence: Follows argument changes, but must order the old publisher's release, the new claims and the topology counts, and a claim conflict mid-rebind leaves half a binding.

chosen: Bind once, at mount
why: No evidence that pages change these arguments in place; the Flutter idiom for initial-only arguments is a new key. The signal that would have changed my mind: a page whose route argument changes without a remount.

question: How does a topic widget render: read getCurrentValue at every build with the subscription only invalidating, or keep the observed values in its State?

options.label: Render the bus's current value; subscription only invalidates
options.consequence: No copy of the value exists to drift; the first frame needs no delivery; a parent rebuild always renders the latest value.

options.label: Keep observed values in State
options.consequence: A second state holder between topic and UI, the drift Rationale §5.2 item 3 warns of, and the first value must still come from getCurrentValue.

chosen: Render the bus's current value; subscription only invalidates
why: Rationale §5.1 and §5.2 (no interposed state holder), Spec §2.5 (getCurrentValue as the synchronous first read), Guide §7.2's useSyncExternalStore pattern, and bus-api@v1 G17 (the first observed value is the value current at listen, so skipping it renders nothing twice).

question: How does an app say whether a BusProvider owns, and so shuts down, its bus?

options.label: Unnamed constructor owns, BusProvider.value does not
options.consequence: Follows the provider package's .value convention Guide §6.4's Provider<Bus> implies; the root case is the short form.

options.label: A boolean flag
options.consequence: One constructor; a flag defaulting either way hides the shutdown decision.

options.label: A separate lifetime widget
options.consequence: Two widgets to place in the right order for every app and test.

chosen: Unnamed constructor owns, BusProvider.value does not
why: Guide §6.4 names Provider<Bus>; in that package .value never disposes. ADR-003 item 7 needs a widget above every scope binding that shuts the bus down at unmount, which the owning provider at the root is.

question: What ends the coordination domain on Flutter: the owning provider's dispose only, or also AppLifecycleState.detached?

options.label: Owning provider's dispose only
options.consequence: Tests, closed views and torn-down add-to-app views shut down; a mobile process that is killed does not, which is unobservable.

options.label: Also AppLifecycleState.detached
options.consequence: Closer to Spec §11.2's iOS trigger, but detached is entered whenever every view detaches while the engine runs on, so a cached engine that reattaches finds a bus that cannot restart.

chosen: Owning provider's dispose only
why: The SDK documents detached as 'still hosted by a Flutter engine but detached from any host views', a state the app can leave again; Spec §11.2's table has no Flutter row, so the mapping is marked for upstreaming. An owner who wants shutdown on process end on iOS would decide otherwise.

question: Platform routes (the initial route and routes the platform pushes): who turns them into intents?

options.label: The executor forwards them as DeepLink, on by default
options.consequence: No route is ever pushed by name over the router; Guide §3.5's capture works out of the box; an app with its own deep-link capture turns it off.

options.label: Left to the app
options.consequence: A Navigator-based WidgetsApp pushes a platform route by name through onGenerateRoute (P5), which the router cannot represent and which bypasses the guard.

options.label: Opt-in forwarding
options.consequence: Safe only when the app remembers it.

chosen: The executor forwards them as DeepLink, on by default
why: P5 shows WidgetsApp pushes a platform route by name unless an earlier binding observer answers it; P5b shows the observer must be registered before WidgetsApp mounts, which Guide §3.5's order gives. The Owns list names the executor, not deep-link capture, so a careful engineer would have confirmed the scope.

question: Which settings does a router route carry, and who builds the Flutter route?

options.label: App builds the route from (entry, settings); settings named '/' + path carrying the entry; other settings rejected
options.consequence: Apps choose MaterialPageRoute, Cupertino or dialogs; the observer and page source read the entry; web and the engine see an absolute route name.

options.label: Adapter builds a PageRouteBuilder around an app widget builder
options.consequence: Less app code, but no Material or Cupertino transitions without depending on those libraries.

options.label: Name equal to the path, no leading slash
options.consequence: Matches NavRoute.path, but WidgetsApp reports the top route's name to the engine as a URI, where a relative name is wrong.

chosen: App builds the route from (entry, settings); settings named '/' + path carrying the entry; other settings rejected
why: WidgetsApp's Navigator reports route names to the engine (reportsRouteUpdateToEngine), and Flutter route names conventionally begin with '/'; the settings check makes the observer's pathOf and the page source reliable.

question: How does the router treat routes it did not build (dialogs, sheets, app pushes)?

options.label: Not entries; a perform pops the ones above the top entry first
options.consequence: Their push and pop confirm nothing; after a perform the top entry's route is the Navigator's top.

options.label: Treat them as entries
options.consequence: They have no NavigationEntry to confirm.

options.label: Remove them silently with removeRoute
options.consequence: Skips their pop transitions and leaves their futures to complete unusually.

chosen: Not entries; a perform pops the ones above the top entry first
why: P7 shows a dialog is an observed push of an unnamed route and popUntil on a route identity pops it; navigation-api@v1 G18 confirms only stack changes.

question: The executor's default name.

options.label: flutter-navigation
options.consequence: Its source renders executor:flutter-navigation, as Spec §2.4's example and Guide §3.4 show.

options.label: navigation
options.consequence: NavigationExecutor's own default; two platforms' executors would share one source.

chosen: flutter-navigation
why: Spec §2.4's example publisher is 'executor:flutter-navigation'.

question: What does the widget-test library offer, given it may import neither test framework and so takes no WidgetTester?

options.label: WidgetTestBus: bus, recorder, input, stub, wrap
options.consequence: Mirrors TestBus's input and stub with ServiceSource('test'), so tests read alike on the VM and in widgets; wrap's owning provider does the ADR-003 item 7 shutdown.

options.label: Only a wrap helper
options.consequence: Every widget test re-creates recorder and stub plumbing.

options.label: A pump helper taking a WidgetTester
options.consequence: Needs package:flutter_test, which ADR-002 item 4 forbids.

chosen: WidgetTestBus: bus, recorder, input, stub, wrap
why: ADR-002 item 4, ADR-003 item 7 and bus-testing@v1 G18 and 'How a test uses it'. It rejects a VirtualSchedulerProvider because tester.pump would not move its clock (ADR-003 item 7).

question: What is the module-scope binding mechanism on Flutter?

options.label: A NavigatorObserver subclass
options.consequence: Sees push, pop, remove and replace on any Navigator; needs nothing of RouteObserver's RouteAware subscriptions.

options.label: A RouteObserver subclass
options.consequence: The Spec's word, but its added API (RouteAware subscribe) is unused here.

options.label: A wrapper widget on the subtree, as React does
options.consequence: Contradicts Spec §7.3's Flutter row.

chosen: A NavigatorObserver subclass
why: Spec §7.3's Flutter row is 'RouteObserver plus a route prefix match'; RouteObserver is itself a NavigatorObserver, and the binding needs only the observer callbacks.

question: How does a module prefix match a route path?

options.label: By segments, ignoring a leading '/' and empty segments
options.consequence: 'checkout' matches 'checkout/cart' and '/checkout', not 'checkouts'.

options.label: By string prefix
options.consequence: 'checkout' matches 'checkouts' and fails on a leading '/'.

chosen: By segments, ignoring a leading '/' and empty segments
why: Router routes are named '/' + path and app routes usually begin with '/'; a string prefix gives false matches.

question: A Navigator that unmounts reports no pop of its routes (P6): how are its module references released?

options.label: ModuleScopeObserver.dispose
options.consequence: An app that removes a Navigator for good disposes its observer; the root Navigator ends with the bus, whose shutdown deactivates every scope.

options.label: Nothing
options.consequence: References of a removed nested Navigator leak and keep their modules active.

chosen: ModuleScopeObserver.dispose
why: P6: after unmount the observer's navigator is null and no didPop or didRemove arrived.

question: Which conveniences does v1 leave out?

options.label: Leave out Router-widget integration and web URL sync, nested-Navigator executors, an event-topic listener widget, a BuildContext extension, route restoration
options.consequence: A smaller surface to fixture now; each is a compatible addition later.

options.label: Include them
options.consequence: More surface and fixtures, with no v1 consumer named.

chosen: Leave out Router-widget integration and web URL sync, nested-Navigator executors, an event-topic listener widget, a BuildContext extension, route restoration
why: The Owns list names neither; root D1 names no web target. The owner may want web URL sync, which is the item a careful engineer would have asked about.

question: Which Flutter libraries may the main library import?

options.label: widgets, foundation and services only
options.consequence: Material, Cupertino and custom-design apps all use it without pulling a design library.

options.label: material too
options.consequence: MaterialPageRoute defaults inside the adapter, at the cost of the material dependency for every app.

chosen: widgets, foundation and services only
why: The app's route builder chooses the presentation; material_ui and cupertino_ui are now pub packages (pub.dev, as go_router 18 depends on them), so the design libraries are moving out of the core.

question: What does the contract say about app code that removes or replaces router routes itself?

options.label: Outside the contract; no guarantee
options.consequence: Honest and small; a dev-mode diagnostic stays a v2 candidate.

options.label: Report a dev-mode diagnostic
options.consequence: Needs the router to reach the bus, which it does not hold.

options.label: Resynchronize the stack
options.consequence: There is no intent to confirm such a change with.

chosen: Outside the contract; no guarantee
why: navigation-api@v1's confirmations carry an intent, and no intent describes an external removal.

question: One page widget for topologies and publisher, or two?

options.label: One PageScope with topologies and a publisher
options.consequence: A page binds its scope in one place; the publisher can claim page-scoped state.

options.label: Separate PageTopologies and PagePublisher widgets
options.consequence: Finer control, two widgets to order per page.

chosen: One PageScope with topologies and a publisher
why: Spec §2.4: a publisher bound to a page scope releases its claim with that scope; Spec §5.2 treats a page as one shell component with a topology and publishes.

question: In the executor suite's Flutter binding, is the executor constructed before or after the hosting WidgetsApp is pumped (S12's template pumps first)?

options.label: Construct, then pump
options.consequence: Exercises the production order of Guide §3.5 and G12 in every case.

options.label: Pump, then construct
options.consequence: S12's template; never exercises a router performing before mount.

chosen: Construct, then pump
why: G12 makes construction before mount the supported order, and P1 shows production reaches the executor before any Navigator exists; both orders pass, this one covers more.

question: How do the bindings perform the platform's back?

options.label: The navigation channel's popRoute message
options.consequence: The real path: binding, WidgetsApp.didPopRoute, Navigator.maybePop, PopScope included.

options.label: navigatorKey.currentState.maybePop()
options.consequence: S12's template; skips WidgetsApp and the binding.

options.label: binding.handlePopRoute()
options.consequence: @protected and @visibleForTesting, so an analyzer diagnostic in a fixture.

chosen: The navigation channel's popRoute message
why: P4 shows popRoute through WidgetsApp pops the top route, never the root, and honors PopScope.

question: How does a conformance library that imports no flutter_test observe the tree?

options.label: Harness methods for the tester's operations; cases observe through their own widgets, builder callbacks and NavigatorObservers
options.consequence: No finder types cross the harness; the suite stays bindable under any runner that can pump.

options.label: Expose finders through the harness
options.consequence: Leaks flutter_test types into the harness interface.

chosen: Harness methods for the tester's operations; cases observe through their own widgets, builder callbacks and NavigatorObservers
why: ADR-001 item 4: a conformance library imports neither test package; earlier contracts' harnesses abstract time and runner the same way.

question: Where does topics.yaml live and what does it generate: one Dart file per domain (Guide C.3's auth_topics.dart), one library per schema file, or one schema file per domain?

options.label: one library per schema file at lib/topics.yaml to lib/topics.g.dart
options.consequence: build_runner can express it (outputs are fixed by the input path); Spec §4.5's single multi-domain file stays; app code still reads AuthTopics.state; diverges from Guide C.3's per-domain file name

options.label: one file per domain from one schema file
options.consequence: matches Guide C.3, but no build_runner builder can name outputs after domains read from inside the input, so build_runner and the command could not write the same files (ADR-002 item 8)

options.label: one schema file per domain ({domain}.topics.yaml to {domain}_topics.dart)
options.consequence: build_runner can express it, but splits Spec §4.5's single source of truth, and two files in different directories could declare one domain

chosen: one library per schema file at lib/topics.yaml to lib/topics.g.dart
why: Spec §4.5 has one topics.yaml with many domains, Guide C.2 asks for build_runner integration, and ADR-002 item 8 requires the builder and the command to write identical bytes; only one output per input satisfies all three. The ^lib/topics.yaml build extension was run on the pinned build 4.0.11 and build_runner 2.16.1 (T5): it applies to lib/topics.yaml only and writes the command's bytes. Guide C.3's per-domain file is informative; marked for upstreaming.

question: What does topics.yaml's initial hold? Spec §4.5's example values (Initializing, empty) are not Dart.

options.label: a Dart expression string, or a YAML number, boolean or null written as the Dart literal
options.consequence: unambiguous and total: any initial value the topic-model constructors accept can be written; the Spec's example values become identifiers that must be in scope; Dart-specific

options.label: a token resolved against the type (Initializing as AuthState.initializing)
options.consequence: reads like the Spec's example and is platform-neutral, but the generator cannot tell a constructor from a static field or an enum value without resolving types, so the output would not compile reliably

options.label: a Dart expression string only
options.consequence: simplest rule, but initial: 0 and initial: false, the natural YAML, would be rejected

chosen: a Dart expression string, or a YAML number, boolean or null written as the Dart literal
why: The generator is a pure function over YAML with no type resolution, so only an expression it copies verbatim always compiles when the author's expression does. Accepting number, boolean and null literals keeps the natural YAML for primitive topics; probe/yaml_facts.out.txt shows how package:yaml 3.1.4 types each scalar, including that an empty value is null and .inf is a non-finite double, which R4 rejects. The Spec's schema is shared across platforms and says nothing about what initial holds; marked for upstreaming. Signal that would change it: a second platform port, which would need a platform-neutral initial value form.

question: How does a topics document say which Dart libraries declare its types?

options.label: per-domain dart.imports list
options.consequence: imports travel with the domain a team owns; the Dart-only key is namespaced, so the schema can stay every platform's source

options.label: top-level imports list
options.consequence: simpler, but the name would be claimed by Dart for every later platform, and imports detach from the domains that need them

options.label: builder options in build.yaml plus command arguments
options.consequence: keeps the YAML platform-neutral, but two configuration sources would have to agree for the builder and the command to write identical bytes

chosen: per-domain dart.imports list
why: Spec §4.5 and Guide C.3 make the schema file the single source for every platform's generator; a namespaced key keeps that, and one source keeps ADR-002 item 8's identical bytes. No evidence distinguishes per-domain from top-level beyond ownership: domains have owners (Spec Appendix A.9).

question: Does the topics document reject unknown keys, or ignore them?

options.label: closed: every unknown key is an error
options.consequence: a misspelled sensitve: true fails instead of silently leaving a sensitive topic unflagged; a later key is a compatible addition for the generator

options.label: open: unknown keys ignored
options.consequence: a later platform's keys pass unchanged, but a typo in sensitive or tracing is silent

chosen: closed: every unknown key is an error
why: Spec §9.2 makes the sensitive flag the privacy gate; a silently ignored misspelling would publish a sensitive topic to every observer. topology-ir@v1's schema is closed for the same kind of reason.

question: Does the file contract also carry a JSON Schema for topics.yaml with valid/ and invalid/ cases, and in which syntax are the cases written?

options.label: schema with JSON-syntax cases, plus rejected/ YAML for the generator-only rules
options.consequence: the format is machine-checkable and editor-usable; the replay tool's schema set runs it with no YAML parser; rules JSON Schema cannot state (repeated keys, collisions, reserved words, non-finite numbers) get YAML inputs the producer's gates use

options.label: schema with YAML cases
options.consequence: cases read like real topics.yaml, but nidana_contract_check would need package:yaml, a dependency outside ADR-002's table that nidana.model would have to add

options.label: no schema, the file replay only
options.consequence: fewer artifacts, but the accepted format would be stated only in prose and one input tree, and invalid inputs would have no fixture at all

chosen: schema with JSON-syntax cases, plus rejected/ YAML for the generator-only rules
why: ADR-001 item 6 gives a file contract one input tree, which cannot show what is rejected; a schema set with invalid cases is the only executable form ADR-001 has for that (item 5). JSON is YAML 1.2, so the cases are also generator inputs (T8: all 4 valid accepted, all 53 invalid rejected with exit 1). The schema compiled and classified every case as marked under package:json_schema 5.2.2 and strict Ajv 8.17.1 (T6, T7); its variant rules were restructured from not/required to properties: false so strict Ajv compiles it.

question: What exact Dart shape does a generated registry member take?

options.label: static final with the type written on the field and the constructor, non-default arguments only, no collections
options.consequence: one form for every variant; nothing inferred, so topic-model@v1's MultiWriterTopic LUB change cannot reach generated code; minimal arguments

options.label: static const for event and replay topics, static final for state topics
options.consequence: event and replay topics usable in const contexts, at the cost of two forms; state topics cannot be const because initial is an arbitrary expression

options.label: inferred field types as Guide C.3 writes them (static final state = StateTopic<AuthState>(...))
options.consequence: shorter, but leaves the field type to inference, which S10's note asks generated code to avoid

chosen: static final with the type written on the field and the constructor, non-default arguments only, no collections
why: topic-model@v1 allows static const or static final in an abstract final class; Guide C.3 shows static final; topics compare by value (topic-model@v1 G7), so const identity buys nothing a registry needs. The S10 note concerns inferred collection element types; generating no collection and writing every type out removes inference altogether. The generated library analyzed clean under lints/recommended, strict modes and --fatal-infos (T4).

question: How are class and member names derived, and what happens when a key cannot become a Dart identifier?

options.label: camel-case derivation, and reject collisions, reserved words and Object member names (R2, R3)
options.consequence: the identifier always reads as the key; a bad key is an error the author fixes once

options.label: camel-case derivation with mangling (switch to switch_, a numeric suffix on collision)
options.consequence: never rejects, but names stop being predictable from the key, and the mangled form trips non_constant_identifier_names

chosen: camel-case derivation, and reject collisions, reserved words and Object member names (R2, R3)
why: probe/names/output.txt compiled a static member under each of 70 candidate names: exactly the 33 reserved words and hashCode, runtimeType, toString, noSuchMethod fail; every built-in and contextual identifier compiles. Rejecting exactly that set is the smallest rule under which every accepted document generates compiling code.

question: How is a description rendered into a doc comment and the catalog?

options.label: Markdown, with < and > outside code spans backslash-escaped
options.consequence: authors keep code spans; raw angle brackets never read as HTML, so the library stays clean under --fatal-infos and the catalog carries no HTML

options.label: Markdown verbatim
options.consequence: a description such as 'emits List<int>' trips unintended_html_in_doc_comment, an INFO that fails every --fatal-infos gate

options.label: plain text, every Markdown character escaped
options.consequence: always safe, but code spans the author writes would show their backticks

chosen: Markdown, with < and > outside code spans backslash-escaped
why: probe/doc/output.txt: the lint reports only the raw <int>; a code span, a backslash escape, a comparison with spaces and an autolink pass. Escaping outside code spans keeps the author's Markdown and the gate clean.

question: What does the topic catalog topics.md contain and how are graph topics matched to document topics?

options.label: per-domain and per-topic sections with property tables, readers and writers from the graph matched by name, plus topology, claim and outside-topic sections
options.consequence: covers Spec Appendix A.9's list (types, sensitivity, owners, readers and writers with scopes); hand-written registries' topics appear from the graph

options.label: one flat table of topics
options.consequence: compact, but descriptions and reader lists do not fit table cells

chosen: per-domain and per-topic sections with property tables, readers and writers from the graph matched by name, plus topology, claim and outside-topic sections
why: Spec Appendix A.9 and Guide §5.2 item 5 list what a catalog shows, including the topologies that read and write each topic and their scopes; Guide C.3 asks for cross-references. Matching by name, not type, because a graph's TopicRef.typeName is the runtime rendering while the document holds the author's text (topology-ir@v1). No evidence beyond the Spec's list decides the layout.

question: How does the build-time topology graph page (Guide C.4) render the graph?

options.label: static HTML embedding topology-ir@v1's Mermaid rendering, Mermaid 11.12.0 loaded from jsDelivr when opened
options.consequence: small, byte-stable page; reuses a rendering topology-ir@v1 already pins; needs network to draw, and shows the readable diagram text offline

options.label: inline the Mermaid library into every page
options.consequence: renders offline, but each generated page carries megabytes of third-party code

options.label: SVG laid out at build time
options.consequence: renders offline with no script, but needs Graphviz or a layout engine in the build, which is global tooling

chosen: static HTML embedding topology-ir@v1's Mermaid rendering, Mermaid 11.12.0 loaded from jsDelivr when opened
why: The build itself needs no network and no global tool; the page's pre text equals topology-ir@v1's render/checkout.mmd golden byte for byte after jsdom's HTML parsing, and Mermaid 11.12.0 parses it (T7). A careful engineer would ask whether the owner's docs must render offline (an external network resource at view time); the signal that would change it is that requirement.

question: Which commands does nidana_dart_codegen expose for this contract, with which arguments and exit codes?

options.label: generate [--graph <graph>] <topics> <output> (pure) and catalog <package>... <output> (runs topology code), exit 0, 1 for rejected input, 2 for usage
options.consequence: the replayable part is a pure function of two files; the graph document is the seam between the catalog run and the documents; one exit-code convention for both

options.label: one command reading an app package and writing everything
options.consequence: one invocation, but nothing is replayable until OQ-T1's mechanism exists, and the docs could not be generated from a graph built elsewhere

chosen: generate [--graph <graph>] <topics> <output> (pure) and catalog <package>... <output> (runs topology code), exit 0, 1 for rejected input, 2 for usage
why: ADR-001 item 6 needs a generator command over an input tree; ADR-002 item 8 names a generator command and leaves names, arguments and exit codes to this contract; Spec §6.5's Catalog.scanTopologies takes a list of packages. The stand-in's exit codes held for every case (T8, T9, T11); T11 first exited 255 because head closed the pipe, an artifact of the script, fixed by capturing to a file.

question: Must this contract fix any part of OQ-T1 (how Catalog.scanTopologies obtains every TopologyDefinition without reflection)?

options.label: fix the output and the definitions' origin only: topology-graph.json holds buildDefinition() of the registered topologies, recorded on the VM unobfuscated; leave registration to the decomposition
options.consequence: consumers can mock against a fixed document; the decomposition keeps every discovery mechanism; catalog's guarantees are not executable here until it picks one

options.label: also fix the registration form now (for example an explicit list the app writes)
options.consequence: catalog would get a replay case, but this step would decide nidana.tooling's open question before its decomposition and before nidana-checks@v1, which shares the scan

options.label: fix nothing about the catalog
options.consequence: topology-ir@v1's Boundary assigns topology-graph.json's path and generator to this contract, which would stay unnamed

chosen: fix the output and the definitions' origin only: topology-graph.json holds buildDefinition() of the registered topologies, recorded on the VM unobfuscated; leave registration to the decomposition
why: Spec §6.5 states the catalog instantiates topology classes and calls buildDefinition(), so the static and runtime graphs are structurally identical; topology-ir@v1 assigns this contract the path and generator and requires a VM run without --obfuscate. How topologies are found, how constructor arguments are supplied, and how Flutter-importing libraries load are mechanism, owned by the decomposition (OQ-T1 Waits on). probe/flutter-vm shows dart run cannot load a library that imports Flutter (dart:ui missing) while flutter test can, which the decomposition must handle.

question: Does topology-graph.json hold shell claims, and from where?

options.label: yes, the claims nidana-checks@v1's workspace scan resolves; unresolvable ones left out with a warning
options.consequence: the published graph is the one the single-writer and scope checks analyze; the claim recognizer is shared with S16

options.label: topologies only
options.consequence: simpler catalog, but topology-ir@v1 defines the catalog's graph with claims, and shell-owned state topics would show no writer

chosen: yes, the claims nidana-checks@v1's workspace scan resolves; unresolvable ones left out with a warning
why: Spec §3.11: the same scan feeds the topology graph generator, where publisher claims appear as source nodes; topology-ir@v1 Refinement 3 builds the catalog's graph from every topology and claim the workspace declares; Spec §3.11 leaves unresolvable write sets to the runtime with a warning.

question: One input/expected pair, as ADR-001 item 6 reads, or several cases?

options.label: one input/expected pair, with a graph, covering every feature in one document
options.consequence: matches ADR-001 item 6 literally, so the replay tool needs nothing new; the no-graph and failure behaviors are not executable and fall to nidana.tooling's gates

options.label: case subdirectories input/{case}/ and expected/{case}/
options.consequence: more behaviors replayable, but the replay tool would implement a layout ADR-001 does not state

chosen: one input/expected pair, with a graph, covering every feature in one document
why: ADR-001 item 6 names one command over input/ compared with expected/, while item 7 gives cli contracts per-case directories; writing a layout the replay tool's author would not find in ADR-001 risks a structure failure at the first replay. Signal that would change it: an ADR-001 amendment adding cases and an expected exit code to file contracts, which would make G2, G14 and G19 executable.

question: Does the generator format its Dart itself, given the replay formats anyway?

options.label: format with package:dart_style at language 3.13
options.consequence: committed registries pass a format check; build_runner and the command format alike; the replay's own format pass is a no-op

options.label: emit unformatted text and rely on the replay's fvm dart format
options.consequence: less code, but a committed lib/topics.g.dart would fail any format check in a gate

chosen: format with package:dart_style at language 3.13
why: ADR-002 lists dart_style among nidana_dart_codegen's dependencies; the stand-in's dart_style 3.1.14 output was unchanged by the SDK's fvm dart format (T1, T2).

question: Is a domain's owner required?

options.label: required
options.consequence: every catalog row names an owning team; a one-person app writes one owner line per domain

options.label: optional
options.consequence: less friction for small apps, but catalog rows without an owner

chosen: required
why: Spec Appendix A.9 lists owning teams from the schema's owner field as part of the catalog, and every example in Spec §4.5 and Guide C.3 carries one. A requirement can be relaxed compatibly later; the reverse is breaking.

question: Which outputs does the build_runner builder write?

options.label: the registry library only
options.consequence: the builder is per input and pure; topics.md and the page, which need the graph, come only from generate

options.label: the registry and topics.md
options.consequence: a catalog without readers and writers next to the source, differing from generate's catalog, which ADR-002 item 8's identical-bytes rule forbids for shared outputs

chosen: the registry library only
why: The catalog's cross references need the graph, which only a catalog run produces; a builder output under lib/ that names topologies would also sit in an importable location, against Spec §4.6 and Guide C.5.

question: Frontmatter: consumers, external consumers, governance.

options.label: consumers [nidana.integration], three external consumers, Governed by ADR-001 and ADR-002
options.consequence: as the root contract matrix names; ADR-003 does not list this contract

options.label: also list nidana-checks@v1's scan as a consumer
options.consequence: the scan is produced by the same node, so it is not a contract edge

chosen: consumers [nidana.integration], three external consumers, Governed by ADR-001 and ADR-002
why: Root contract matrix row topic-codegen@v1; ADR-001 and ADR-002 affects lists include topic-codegen@v1; node ids with phase_ids provisional until reconcile.

question: Which v1 checks are plugin rules and which are scan checks?

options.label: ADR-002 split
options.consequence: per-library checks (raw-string topic, global accessor, sensitive flag, explicit type arguments) report in the IDE and dart analyze; aggregate checks (uniqueness, single-writer, cycles, self-reference, scope) run in the scan over the IR

options.label: everything in the scan
options.consequence: one host and one output format, but no IDE feedback for per-library misuse, and ADR-002 item 7 already places those checks in the plugin

chosen: ADR-002 split
why: ADR-002 items 7 and 8 fix the split: a plugin rule sees one library, the aggregate checks need the model's analyses, which the plugin cannot depend on. The contract restates it as Refinement 1 so consumers need not read the ADR.

question: What severity does each plugin rule report at by default?

options.label: blocking rules WARNING, sensitivity INFO
options.consequence: plain fvm dart analyze fails (exit 2) on raw-string topics, global accessors and explicit type arguments, and only --fatal-infos fails it on an unflagged sensitive type, matching root D1's 'as a warning'

options.label: all INFO (LintCode default)
options.consequence: app CI running plain dart analyze never fails on any nidana rule; only --fatal-infos blocks, and then the sensitivity warning blocks too

options.label: blocking rules ERROR
options.consequence: red squiggles and exit 3 for lint-like checks; WARNING already fails dart analyze by default

chosen: blocking rules WARNING, sensitivity INFO
why: analyzer 13.3.0's LintCode takes a severity and the plugin server reports the declared severity unless the diagnostics section overrides it (read in analysis_server_plugin 0.3.18 plugin_server.dart, confirmed by the experiment's analyze-* cases). WARNING is how the analyzer marks blocking static problems; INFO is the only default that keeps a check informative under plain dart analyze. Apps can raise the sensitivity rule to error per diagnostic, which is Guide C.1's v2 configurable error, already available.

question: How are diagnostic codes named, and what do the messages say?

options.label: unprefixed snake case
options.consequence: raw_string_topic, global_bus_accessor, explicit_topic_type_arguments, unflagged_sensitive_topic; suppression reads // ignore: nidana_dart_lint/raw_string_topic

options.label: nidana_ prefix
options.consequence: codes identifiable in dart analyze output without the plugin name, but suppression reads nidana_dart_lint/nidana_raw_string_topic

chosen: unprefixed snake case
why: the analysis server qualifies plugin codes by plugin name in ignore comments, so a prefix repeats it. Messages name the offending literal, name, method or type and give one correction each; the scan's codes follow the same style. Close call: the signal for the prefix would be a second plugin in app CI with clashing codes.

question: What is a raw-string topic use on Dart, where no bus method takes a string?

options.label: literal name outside a static-field initializer
options.consequence: reports topic creations named by a string literal anywhere but as the whole initializer of a static field; top-level variables are reported; non-literal names pass

options.label: any creation outside a registry
options.consequence: also catches names passed through variables, but reports the tree's own generic helpers and decoders, which ADR-002 says the rules must accept

options.label: accept top-level variables too
options.consequence: small apps may declare topics top-level, but Spec §4.4 asks for registry classes and the uniqueness scan is the only remaining guard

chosen: literal name outside a static-field initializer
why: Spec §4.2 and §4.4 forbid naming a topic by string at a use site and organize topics in registry classes; topic-model@v1 says registries are static members. Restricting to literal names keeps every legitimate construction in the tree's own lib code clean (ADR-002 Consequences). The signal that would have changed it: an owner preference for top-level registries.

question: What counts as a global bus accessor?

options.label: variables, static fields and getters
options.consequence: top-level variables, static fields, top-level getters and static getters of type Bus or a subclass, nullable or not

options.label: variables and static fields only
options.consequence: bus-api@v1's wording; a static getter returning a cached bus would pass

chosen: variables, static fields and getters
why: Spec §3.1's example is Bus.instance, which on Dart is as often a static getter as a field; a getter reaches a bus without a reference exactly as a field does. Functions that create a bus are not accessors and pass.

question: Is a check against explicit type arguments on publish a v1 rule (S13's suggestion)?

options.label: v1 rule over four sinks
options.consequence: explicit_topic_type_arguments reports explicit type arguments on Bus.publish, Publisher.publish, TopologyBuilder.write and reduceInto, closing bus-api@v1 G40's stated gap and the same gap in topology-dsl@v1; root D1's check list and nidana.tooling's Owns line need a matching touch

options.label: defer
options.consequence: Spec §4.2's compile-time type check keeps a covariance hole on Dart that no v1 package or check enforces, which root's first success criterion requires to be listed as deferred in D1

chosen: v1 rule over four sinks
why: root's first success criterion requires every normative Dart-applicable rule to be implemented, enforced or deferred in D1; G40 records that the package does not fully implement Spec §4.2. The rule is per-library, trivial and cheaper than an amendment to D1. Extending it to write and reduceInto follows the same covariance (topology-dsl@v1 G3). Would have asked: it adds a check beyond the owner-approved D1 list.

question: What is a known-sensitive type, and where is Spec §9.2's configurable list?

options.label: suffixes plus a Sensitive annotation on types and aliases
options.consequence: Token, Credential, Credentials, PaymentInfo suffixes, any annotation whose class is named Sensitive, on the type or the alias it is written through, at any depth of type arguments and record fields; apps mark third-party types through an annotated typedef; no options file

options.label: a list file the plugin reads
options.consequence: a true keyword list, but analysis_server_plugin 0.3.18 gives rules no options, the file would sit outside the analysis server's invalidation, and IDE results would go stale

options.label: a Sensitive declaration in nidana_dart_contracts
options.consequence: one canonical annotation, but a topic-model@v1 amendment before this contract stands

chosen: suffixes plus a Sensitive annotation on types and aliases
why: Spec §9.2 names the suffixes *Token, *Credential, *PaymentInfo and @Sensitive types plus a configurable list; Spec §4.5's own example flags LoginCredentials, hence the plural suffix. The plugin API has no plugin options (read in analysis_server_plugin 0.3.18 plugin_server.dart: only per-diagnostic severities are configurable), so the configurable list is expressed in code, which the IDE re-analyzes live. Recognizing Sensitive by class name from any library needs no contract amendment now and keeps working if topic-model@v1 later declares one. Would have asked: the form of the configurable list is an owner preference.

question: Which code do the checks read?

options.label: outside test directories
options.consequence: every library outside test/, integration_test/, test_driver/ and testing/ (RuleContext.isInTestDirectory), in both hosts; test code may claim, stub and declare ad hoc topics

options.label: lib/ only
options.consequence: misses bin/, tool/ and example/ code that wires a bus

options.label: everything
options.consequence: every test's TestBus stub claim and ad hoc topic is reported, and the tree's own tests fail the root analyze gate

chosen: outside test directories
why: bus-api@v1 already speaks of 'application code'; the analyzer's own test-directory definition makes the plugin and the scan agree, and test code claims topics on purpose (bus-testing@v1, flutter-binding@v1 G17).
evidence: analyzer 13.3.0 RuleContext.isInTestDirectory and workspace.dart test directory names
docs/auto-run/experiments/nidana-checks-fixtures/ (analyze-clean, scan-clean, seeded defects D1 and D4)

question: Which constructs in application code are claim sites?

options.label: four sites
options.consequence: Bus.publisher, PageScope(writes:), NavigationExecutor and FlutterNavigationExecutor; an app topology writing nav.current-route is caught at merge

options.label: Bus.publisher and PageScope
options.consequence: the executors' claims sit inside library code the app does not scan, so a second writer of nav.current-route surfaces only at activation

options.label: Bus.publisher only
options.consequence: the Spec's wording, but flutter-binding@v1 G7 makes PageScope a claim in app code

chosen: four sites
why: S14 found PageScope(writes:) to be a second claim site; navigation-api@v1 G19 and flutter-binding@v1 G14 fix the executors' claim (nav.current-route, application scope, executor source with a default name), which Spec §3.11 names as the canonical shell-owned state topic.

question: When does a claim's write set or scope resolve statically, and what happens otherwise?

options.label: set literal of declared state topics; else warning and left out
